title: Breaking: SA government commits $109m to help struggling wine industry
text:
Tell us about your experience.

The South Australian government has announced a $109 million support package for the state's struggling wine industry.

Grape growers across Australia have pleaded for support since the pandemic, when the industry experienced a major glut of red wine due to a ban on exports of Australian wines to China and a global downturn in wine consumption.

SA is home to several major wine regions, including the Barossa Valley, McLaren Vale and the Riverland.

Premier Peter Malinauskas announced the package today with $100 million dedicated to loans to help growers transition to other crops.

He said eligible growers would be able to access loans of up to $500,000, with no principal or interest repayments required for the first two years.

The support package also includes a two-year extension of the Global Wine Growth Program to drive international demand, support the disposal of chemically treated wine posts and address wine surplus inventories.

title: Japan lifts interest rates to counter 'shocking' inflation
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Japan was the country that inflation forgot.

But after almost 30 years of 0 per cent interest rates, things are changing.

The Bank of Japan today increased rates to 1.25 per cent in a widely anticipated move to counter inflation fuelled by high energy costs.

It comes on the back of a rate rise in June, which bumped rates up to 1 per cent, the highest rate Japan has seen since 1995.

Another rise, just three months later, marks the shortest time between increases since 1990.

In announcing the decision, the Bank of Japan pointed to the situation in the Middle East, growing demand for AI products, and exchange rate fluctuations.

Japan's current inflation rate of about 2 per cent has shocked some in the country. (AFP: Toru Yamanaka)

Inflation in Japan is currently sitting at close to 2 per cent, but the central bank is concerned about it potentially rising further.

While that may seem low by Australian standards, macroeconomist Fujiwara Ippei, a professor at Keio University and the University of Tokyo, said even 2 per cent inflation was "maybe shocking" for some people in Japan.

"Two per cent is not so large, but we are so used to 0 per cent," Professor Fujiwara said.

Fujiwara Ippei says some are struggling with the higher inflation because they have used to 0 per cent rates. (ABC News: Natalie Whiting)

Interest rates in Japan were aggressively cut in the 1990s in the wake of the country's asset bubble burst in the 1990s and the period of low growth that followed.

In 2013, the Bank of Japan set a goal of a stable 2 per cent inflation to pull the country out of deflation. A range of monetary policies, including increased money supply and negative interest rates, were used to encourage spending.

But the current inflation is being driven by supply shocks — rising import and production costs.

Global economic policy is at the mercy of Bessent's to-do list Global economic policy now seems at the mercy of an exceptionally casual approach to information, scribbled on a notepad, awaiting an update on Scott Bessent's to-do list.

Inflation started increasing in 2021 on the back of the COVID-19 pandemic and then the wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, at times edging toward 3 per cent. In 2024, the Bank of Japan began a program of gradual rate rises to "normalise" the economy.

Professor Fujiwara said "a zero-inflation norm is really tricky" because people got used to nominal prices for things like lunch.

"The price of lunch didn't change [from] when I was a university student 30 years ago," he said.

"So suddenly we see the increase, so therefore the people are really frustrated."

With inflation persisting and Japan's rates so low, the prevailing market view appears to be that the hikes will continue after today.

Washington's watchful eye

Japan's central bank will also be keen to try to support the yen, which recently hit a 40-year low against the US dollar, prompting joint yen-buying intervention from the US and Japan.

US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent defended the move by saying a stronger yen was "better for American exporters" and meant the Japanese government did "not have to sell US assets".

"I am the house now, so when we intervene with the Japanese yen, I have pretty good insight into what … what Japanese policymakers are going to do," he said last week.

The depreciating yen recently sparked an intervention by the Trump administration. (Kyodo via Reuters)

The US Federal Reserve voted on Wednesday, local time, to raise rates to between 3.75 and four per cent, and the European Central Bank announced an increase last week.

The depreciated yen is also adding to inflation by increasing the cost of imports.

The decision about rates has implications outside the country, as traders often borrow cheaply in Japan and invest the money into higher-yielding assets elsewhere.

Scott Bessent says a stronger-valued yen is "better for American exporters". (Reuters: Sam Wolfe)

Professor Fujiwara, who worked at the Bank of Japan for almost two decades, said the overt pressure to raise rates from the US was "quite unusual", but he believed the Bank of Japan would have made the decision to raise today's rate regardless.

"But if there is further pressure from the United States — it's important for the central bank that they are making a decision independently," he said.

" They don't want to have some impression that their decision is influenced by the government or influenced by a foreign government. "

He said the increase to 1.25 per cent today was "reasonable" and if it had not happened, the Bank of Japan would risk sending the wrong sign to the market.

Future interest rate rises could be more contentious, in part because Japan's government debt-to-GDP ratio is above 200 per cent, significantly higher than most advanced economies.

"Bank of Japan may be confident, but I'm not so sure about whether the current 2 per cent inflation level can persist or not because of the sluggish real-wage developments," he said.

"And also, when they increase the interest rate to fight inflation, they need to worry about the impact to the government bond market."

The Bank of Japan today said it would continue to "raise the policy interest rate and adjust the degree of monetary easing" in response to economic and price conditions.

It said it would consider the "timing and pace of these adjustments" while assessing the likelihood of stabilising the underlying inflation rate at about 2 per cent and the "associated risks".

More than 100,000 people aged over 100 in Japan

At Jizō-dōri, a shopping strip in Tokyo colloquially known as "Granny's Harujuku" because of its popularity with the older generation, shoppers told the ABC they were feeling the pinch of inflation.

Yoshikawa san, 69, said she has noticed price rises on everyday items like detergent and food.

"I can't get by on my pension alone, so I'm doing part-time work," she said.

"It's all a bit of a mess. The amount I receive just isn't enough."

Yoshikawa san, 69, says she is now working part-time to survive. (ABC News: Natalie Whiting)

She is far from alone, with many inside Japan calling for further increases to pension rates to keep up with the cost of living.

The Japanese government will cut a tax on food for two years from next April to help people, but the decision has sparked concern that it risks creating a budget shortfall.

The Japanese government is pushing an expansionary fiscal policy — using public spending and cuts taxes to stimulate economic growth, which would then reduce the debt-to-GDP ratio.

There are now more than 100,000 people in Japan aged more than 100 years old. (Reuters: Issei Kato)

But analysts say its success will hinge on market confidence, and without that, it could trigger increases in long-term interest rates and a weakening of the yen.

And inflation is not the only fiscal challenge Japan is facing.

This week Japan reported there are now more than 100,000 people in the country who are more than 100 years old.

Shoppers at Tokyo's Jizō-dōri shopping strip have told the ABC they are feeling the pinch of inflation. (ABC News: Natalie Whiting)

The high rate of centurions is a credit to the population's health, but it also speaks to Japan's aging society, which will add to the financial pressure the country is facing.

"What is worrisome in the future is that … we are an aging society, but we will enter the super-aging society," Professor Fujiwara said.

"So eventually, the medical cost and nursing care costs will increase massively."

Loading

He said government expenditure would have to increase, but he questioned where the debt could be absorbed by consumers.

"It's going to be a very tough situation."

title: How the NRL's most underrated player explains the Knights
text:
In the modern rugby league landscape it's hard for any NRL player to be truly underrated.

Coverage of the game is more granular and intense than ever before and the rise of fantasy sports means every statistical contribution comes into focus, which makes it difficult for anyone to slide under the radar.

But Mat Croker, the man who explains how Newcastle have managed to find themselves in a sudden-death final against the Warriors on Sunday, has managed it after putting together a season of low-key excellence that makes him worthy of the title.

Knights win is proof the future has come Stars were born under the finals lights as Newcastle knockout finals win over South Sydney announced the dawn of a new tomorrow.

The lock forward is the only Knight to have played every game this year and his ball-playing in the middle of the field is the straw that stirs the drink for their dynamic attack.

"I'm the link man to our halves and making sure our weapons out wide, guys like KP [Kalyn Ponga] and Braddy [Bradman Best] and Gags [Dane Gagai] get the ball if the cues are there in the defender," Croker said.

"If they're not, just go through the middle."

The 27-year-old makes his job sound simple, and maybe it is, but that's not the same as easy. If it was, someone else would be doing it.

Croker is a microcosm of Newcastle's turnaround from wooden spooners to the brink of the club's first preliminary final since 2013 because, like his team, he knows his strengths and has been empowered to play to them.

There are more explosive and dazzling players at the Knights but Croker's passing, communication and structure helps give them the opportunity to explode and dazzle. He is the rock on which you can build a church that worships attacking football.

Mat Croker has been a fixture at the back of the scrum for Newcastle. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner)

Newcastle lead the league in tries from their own half with 31. More than a quarter of those begin with Croker at first receiver, setting shape and creating time for the men outside him.

Like the other things Croker does well — chasing kicks, leading line speed in defence, slowing down the ruck — his impact in attack is a hard thing to quantify with numbers. But if you know what you're looking for, it becomes impossible to miss.

Sidelined halfback Dylan Brown believes it's invaluable and that Croker is part of the reason the Knights have been able to stay on their feet and make it to the second week of the finals despite a heavy injury toll.

Mat Croker has enjoyed the best season of his NRL career. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne)

"He understands the game really well. His footy smarts, when to play it out the back and when to run — he knows he's not the biggest player on the field but he knows how to find a gap and he knows when the spine needs the ball," said Brown.

"We've had all these new players come in but we still have the core. We still have Mat Croker and Phoenix Crossland, they haven't changed all year, and the more the ball goes through their hands the easier it's going to be for the rest of the team.

"You need that. Every team needs those guys."

It's been a season of great improvement for Croker, who notched his 100th NRL game earlier this year.

Since his debut in 2021 he has been a solid contributor for the Knights and a good clubman who mainly came off the bench, starting just 13 of his 82 appearances prior to this year.

Mat Croker spent much of his early years coming off the bench. (AAP: Darren Pateman)

But after working closely with new coach Justin Holbrook and attack coach Steven Hales over the summer, Croker was given a chance to start in the club's trip to Las Vegas in Round 1.

He has since transformed from honest toiler to a genuine ball-playing lock, a coalfields remix of the sophisticated passing middle that every decent team needs.

"Ever since day one they've put a lot of responsibility on my shoulders and I'm really grateful they've done that because I think it's brought out the best football of my career," Croker said.

"Back in Vegas they backed a hunch and took a bit of a punt of me to start and I've had the luxury of starting every game since. That's a lot of faith and I try to repay it."

The greatest compliment you can pay a middle forward is to say "he's got a bit of footy in him" and Croker has proven he's got more than most.

Newcastle can progress to their first preliminary final since 2013 with a win on Sunday. (Getty Images: Scott Gardiner )

The skills were always there, he just needed the chance to unlock them.

"Without being arrogant, I always felt like I had some skills with passing and I'm not a barnstorming forward, so I had to work around that and find other ways to improve," said Croker.

"The ability to pass and show and go was part of that — the cues, I've worked really hard with Halesy and Justo to see those.

"He's said the same thing to me for 28 games — if they're tight, move it, and if they're not go through it."

In sticking to that mantra, Croker has become to Newcastle what his opposite number on Sunday, reigning Dally M Lock of the Year Erin Clark, is to the Warriors or what Cameron Murray is to last week's vanquished foes, South Sydney.

Croker had a strong game in that one, leading the way for Newcastle's depleted pack by holding the middle together and making 42 tackles without a miss, and says he was inspired by the prospect of taking on Murray.

"I was coming up against a good 13 in Cameron Murray, who's one of the best players in the whole competition," Croker said.

How Knights finals rookie shut down Souths Newcastle was not short of heroes in its sudden-death finals win over South Sydney, but no player stood taller than 21-year-old backrower and play-off debutant Jermaine McEwen.

"I'm not saying I played over him but I knew I had a big challenge because we play similar roles and I tried to embrace that challenge without the two front-rowers I've beside me all year.

"I had to use my leadership a bit more and I'm proud of how I did it."

Repeating the dose against Clark and the Warriors in front of 50,000 fans at Eden Park is a tall order but few dare write the Knights off.

They're dangerous because they've had a whole season of learning how to play to their strengths, like they did against South Sydney and like Croker has all year to become the NRL's hidden gem.

If they pull off the upset, look for Croker at the heart of it and if he is he sure won't stay underrated for long.

title: Door not closed for Socceroos veteran despite another snub
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Mat Ryan's Socceroos days are not over, coach Tony Popovic insists, despite the decorated captain being left out of his first squad since the World Cup.

Ryan is the most eyebrow-raising omission from Popovic's squad, which includes seven uncapped players, for games against Brazil in Brisbane on September 25 and Townsville on September 28.

The 34-year-old lost his starting spot to young goalkeeper Patrick Beach at the World Cup, then was bizarrely substituted on for the round-of-32 penalty shootout against Egypt.

The Socceroos skipper, capped 105 times, said after that loss he was only told he might replace Beach as extra time kicked off, though Popovic has since insisted Ryan knew that was a possibility pre-match.

Tony Popovic's Socceroos are set to face Brazil in Brisbane and Townsville. (Stefan Koops/EYE4IMAGES/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Levante goalkeeper Ryan has been omitted despite a strong start to the La Liga season.

"We know what Maty Ryan is to Australian football," Popovic said.

"A player that has a distinguished career, continues to have one, over 100 caps.

"But we'd like to have a look at another keeper."

Pressed on how Ryan, who the Socceroos boss also dropped in his first games in charge in 2024, had taken the omission, Popovic said: "He's good.

"He's the ultimate professional that he is, and that's why he's had such a distinguished career.

"He's still available for us, and he's certainly not out of the picture moving forward."

Uncapped St Mirren goalkeeper Jacob Chapman replaces Ryan, joining Beach and Paul Izzo in the squad.

Untried left-back Kasey Bos, younger brother of injured star Jordan Bos, has been called up along with fellow untested defender Dylan Leonard, 19.

Former A-League sensations Marcus Younis (Brondby IF) and Eli Adams (Gamba Osaka) earn maiden call-ups alongside Kealey Adamson (QPR), Chapman and Yaya Dukuly (NK Celje) after impressive stints overseas.

"They've been rewarded for the hard work they've put in to get an opportunity overseas," Popovic said.

"They've had to go through the struggles when you go outside of your comfort zone.

"You go through the ups and downs; not playing, playing, injuries, and that helps you grow.

"And these players get mentally tougher; they know how to handle the difficult situations in games, and I believe they all deserve an opportunity."

Sixteen players from the 26-man World Cup squad return.

Star left-back Jordan Bos (knee) and central defender Cam Burgess (Achilles) are unavailable.

Court battle looms for Socceroos star Cristian Volpato is set for a court battle as the Socceroos star's lawyer confirms he will challenge charges that he was driving with cocaine in his system.

Cristian Volpato (hamstring) is sidelined with injury.

The Sassuolo attacker was last week fined $722 for driving with cocaine in his system in July. Volpato has maintained his innocence and will challenge the charges in court.

Riley McGree and Patrick Yazbek return after missing the World Cup through injury while Alex Robertson has been recalled.

Cameron Devlin, Nishan Velupillay, Mathew Leckie, Ajdin Hrustic, Kai Trewin and Awer Mabil have been omitted.

Aziz Behich is the only A-League Men player in the squad.

The Socceroos could have played up to four games this window but have settled for two, which Popovic said allowed players to get back to their clubs.

"We feel that with the games in November, we'll be ready for the Asian Cup," he said.

AAP

title: The BOM revamps rain radar on maligned new website
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Almost a year since the launch of its much-maligned new website, the Bureau of Meteorology (BOM) has made major upgrades to rain radar information.

The BOM faced a torrent of criticism over the new-look site, which was launched in October last year during wild weather.

One of the main criticisms was the look and usability of the new rain radar, which forced the bureau to swiftly change the colour scheme of the tool.

The bureau now says it had further improved the weather map to make it easier to find rainfall information.

Chief executive Stuart Minchin said the latest update addressed community feedback.

"We know how much value the community places on their local rain radar," he said.

"We've listened to feedback and made these updates to help you get to your local radar faster and estimate how far away rain is," Dr Minchin said.

Stuart Minchin says the changes were made in response to community feedback. (Supplied: Australian Parliament)

Website drama

It has been a tumultuous year for the national weather forecaster.

Not only was there a big backlash to the look and usability of the new site, the cost of the revamp was also scrutinised and later revealed to have cost taxpayers $96.5 million.

BOM executives were grilled in federal parliament Senate questioning.

In August this year, Dr Minchin announced an independent review.

The new update adds more information to the radar view launched last year. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

While the new website still looks fairly similar to how it did when it first launched, several updates have been done.

The latest round of changes went live this week, including enhancements to the rain radar and weather map.

"This update includes the addition of radar locations, radar quick links [and] changes to how rainfall is displayed," the BOM said in a statement.

"Radar range rings [also] provide a visual measurement guide to how far rainfall is from familiar landmarks and locations."

A radar locations feature, radar quick links and clickable radar icons have also been added.

"Rain is now better detected and more accurately displayed on the weather map, with higher definition and detail when very light to moderate rainfall is observed and when data from overlapping radars is used," the statement said.

Dr Minchin said more updates were planned for later this year, including some changes to Australian places with dual names.

"We encourage the community to continue to share their website feedback, and we will respond with enhancements and adjustments," he said.

title: AI companies would need to report 'rogue' incidents under proposed laws
text:
Tell us about your experience.

AI companies could be legally required to report rogue incidents such as the hacking of another company, under a proposal from the Albanese government as part of its plans for new safety, environmental and industrial rules for the technology.

Data centres already in development but not yet built may also be retrospectively required to comply with a raft of new rules being considered by the government, which includes prioritising the use of recycled water and forcing AI companies to reserve computing capacity for Australian businesses and researchers.

These options have been floated in a new paper from the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet on the proposed national "AI standards", which the federal government hopes to legislate in early 2027.

It sets out the goal of attracting major investment from top AI companies here in a "sustainable" way.

Know more about this story? Email Cam Wilson on wilson.cameron@abc.net.au or his secure email cmwlsn@protonmail.com

"The Australian Government has been clear about the important objective of growing AI capability in Australia. We welcome investment, but on Australia's terms," assistant science minister Andrew Charlton said in a statement.

New rules for 'reportable incidents'

In July, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese announced his government would create a set of national laws and rules about the development of AI and its infrastructure, such as data centres, in Australia.

A discussion paper published today for feedback, said companies authorised to undertake large-scale AI training in Australia would face minimum safety and security requirements, including "disclosing defined reportable AI incidents to relevant Australian authorities".

It did not define what a "reportable incident" would be, but the paper asked for feedback on whether developers should have to provide information proactively, on request, or through public disclosures.

Australia currently has no such rule.

It comes during a period of heightened global scrutiny on AI safety, with leaders of frontier AI companies recently coming out in favour of a coordinated slowing of development.

Over the past few months, several major AI companies and some individuals have disclosed incidents of AI models taking potentially malicious actions without being asked, starting with OpenAI's disclosure that two of its models had gone "rogue" and broken into the systems of AI company Hugging Face.

This week, OpenAI, one of the world's biggest AI companies, reported six incidents of unexpected or concerning behaviour observed during the training or evaluation of its models over the past six months.

Projects already approved could face requirements

The consultation paper also provided more detail about which data centres the standards could apply.

This included opening discussion on whether they should retrospectively apply to projects not yet operational when the rules commence, including those already moving through approvals and development.

The ABC last week identified 27 approved-but-unbuilt data centres, following the prime minister's earlier comments the rules would not apply retrospectively to projects already approved or under construction.

The Albanese government is developing national standards for AI. (ABC News: Adam Kennedy)

Larger facilities would face tougher requirements under proposed capacity tiers, while small centres with electricity connection capacity below 30 megawatts could be excluded.

Projects above a capacity threshold could have to submit compliance plans and confirm they had the necessary building and electricity connection approval.

The discussion paper shows the government also wants large data centres to bring forward enough new renewable energy generation to offset their electricity demand, which can be backed by gas, batteries or hydro to keep supply reliable.

Centres could also have to adjust their electricity demand to support the grid and operate in ways that minimise costs for households and businesses.

Whether electricity use should be matched with renewable generation during particular periods has also been floated, including the idea of requiring matching consumption annually and during some periods with renewable energy certificates.

Unbuilt, but already approved data centres could be forced to comply with the standards. (Reuters: Toby Melville)

For water, the proposed standards would require centres to minimise consumption, prioritise efficient cooling and recycled or non-drinking water, and pay their share of infrastructure and servicing costs.

Data centre providers would also have to prepare for drought and water disruptions, meet efficiency standards and report water use.

Companies training advanced AI here would also be expected to support Australian research, including by paying directly or by reserving computing capacity for their work.

Advocacy group Data Centres Australia chief executive Belinda Dennett welcomed the paper, saying it supported a national framework rather than a patchwork of other regulations.

"The paper asks the right questions, on energy, water, costs and community, and it rightly recognises that this infrastructure has to be built on terms that work for Australians," Ms Dennett said.

Power on the line as data centres boom Australia's biggest wind farm is about to double in capacity. Twenty-five per cent will power data centres.

Anthropic, one of the world's biggest AI companies, and which this week signed a deal with the Queensland government to use part of a proposed $32 billion data centre in the state, welcomed the paper.

"We believe that Australia should have agency in how AI is used and developed. This includes clear rules on how the associated infrastructure is built out. We intend to build to meet these standards and look forward to engaging constructively in this process," the company's ANZ head of policy David Masters said.

Speaking at an AI parliamentary hearing this morning, Department of Industry, Science and Resources deputy secretary Helen Wilson said hosting AI training would give Australia greater influence over the technology.

"By having training here, that does give us the ability to help shape the development and deployment of AI," she said.

Responses to the AI standards consultation paper are due by October 9.

OpenAI, Google and Meta did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: A-League season start under threat with referees on strike
text:
Tell us about your experience.

It is seemingly a rare occurrence indeed that Australian football does not find itself in some degree of turmoil.

So it is perhaps of little surprise that as the A-League Men's and Women's seasons fast approach, the code is once again lurching towards another crisis.

The nations top referees have been on strike since September 4, citing "significant changes to the elite refereeing structure" proposed by Football Australia (FA).

The change would see the referees contracted directly by the league, instead of FA.

The Professional Football Referees Association (PFRA) says those changes would be "detrimental to individual referees and represent a drastic step backwards for the professional refereeing program".

The A-League seasons begin in four weeks. And the parties are, as things stand, at something of a stalemate.

The APL and FA have all told ABC Sport they are continuing to work together with the aim of reaching a resolution.

The referee's body said in a statement earlier this month that it would "continue to engage with Football Australia with the aim of resolving the outstanding matters and returning its members to the field as soon as an acceptable outcome can be reached".

As players and supporters at all levels know, without referees there can be no game, so how have we got here?

Who runs the A-Leagues?

The A-League Men and A-League Women seasons get underway in mid-October. (Getty Images: Hagen Hopkins)

To get into the weeds of this dispute, we can go back to the 2020 decision to decouple the A-League from Football Australia.

FA relinquished full control to a newly formed body, the Australian Professional Leagues, after a long period of agitation from both the clubs and world body FIFA about governance issues within the game.

In practice, this meant handing over the commercial reins of the A-Leagues to the clubs, in line with many other professional football leagues around the world, such as the Premier League, Bundesliga and J-League, among others.

The clubs believed the separation from the national governing body would help the competition's long-term viability.

The reality has been somewhat different.

In 2024, half of A-League Men players said they were "dissatisfied" with how the competition had been managed by the APL, and close to half said they had "low trust" in whether it could improve the league.

That same year, APL slashed the annual distribution to the clubs from close to $2 million to just $530,000 on account of an increasingly worrying financial outlook.

That followed a frankly disastrous plan to sell off grand finals to Sydney and rapidly declining interest and attendances.

Since then, the stalled expansion drive and the removal of failed club Western United and last month's breakdown of talks between the league and the players over the collective bargaining agreement have added to an environment of intense distrust.

Why are the referees on strike?

The referees are not striking about on-field behaviour. (Getty Images: Phil Walter)

Since the league unbundled from Football Australia, the sport's governing body has still provided the referees to the league, with the APL reimbursing FA for those costs.

Now, Football Australia has proposed that it will only pay for matches that come under their jurisdiction: the Australia Cup and Australian Championship.

That means the APL has to pay the referees to officiate its competitions directly, which FA says is the APL's responsibility under the contract it has signed with the league.

However, this is one of the issues that the PFRA has railed against, arguing in essence it would be a conflict of interest to officiate the clubs, who are in effect their employers.

"Such an arrangement would place referees in an unacceptable position of potential conflict and raise serious concerns regarding the integrity and impartiality of the refereeing program," the PFRA said in a statement.

The referees would prefer the formation of an independent referees body, as is the case in England with Pro Ref, formerly known as PGMOL.

The PFRA added that the proposed structure was "untenable" and that referees "cannot grow without trust [or] succeed without independence".

Football Australia said there were no issues around the integrity with their proposal, and that it was consistent with FIFA regulations.

The PFRA also said match officials who officiated in trial matches involving A-League clubs had not been paid their outstanding match fees by FA, which was refuted by FA, which said there were no outstanding debts owed.

Have games been affected?

Referee Rowan Fisher took charge of the Australia Cup semifinal. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Football Australia was forced to fly in four Singaporean referees for the Australia Cup semifinal clash between Sydney FC and Melbourne Victory on September 9.

Young Australian referee Rowan Fisher, who does not have any A-League experience, took charge of the second semifinal between South Melbourne and Lions FC earlier this week.

It is understood that there is no risk of the Australia Cup final between South Melbourne and Melbourne Victory on October 10 not being played.

This is due to a group of referees that have signed a contract with FA despite the stand-off.

The second season of the second-tier Australian Championship, which kicks off on Thursday October 15, is also not expected to be at risk.

Both those competitions are administered by FA.

However, no assurances have been given about the A-Leagues, Men and Women, which both start that same weekend.

'Nobody becomes a referee because they want to withdraw their services'

One could understand the A-League referees not wanting to rush back… (Getty Images: Josh Chadwick)

The nation's referees are clear they want to get back to the business of refereeing.

But they feel their voices need to be heard.

"Our members have delivered an overwhelmingly clear message. They are seeking certainty around their employment, payment of outstanding amounts, and a clear and sustainable structure for professional refereeing in Australia," PFRA president Evgeny Vizelman said in a statement.

"We do not take the decision to stop officiating matches lightly. Our members want to officiate football, prepare for the upcoming season and positively contribute to the success of football in Australia.

"Nobody becomes a referee because they want to withdraw their services.

"Taking ourselves off the field hurts. There comes a point where people have to stand together and say the way they are being treated is not good enough."

title: Runaway Tasmanian devil back on display at wildlife park after weeks on the run
text:
Tell us about your experience.

A Tasmanian devil that sparked a two-week search in dense bushland is back on public display at a Gold Coast wildlife park after spending months in recovery following her misadventure.

Mary, the two-year-old escape artist, made headlines in June when she absconded from an enclosure at the Paradise Country park with what staff described at the time as an "abnormally large leap".

The daring devil spent more than two weeks on the run, evading sniffer dogs, thermal drone technology, humane traps and every other attempt to capture her.

She was eventually found in bushland less than 2 kilometres from the park.

Mary then spent the next five days in a specialist wildlife hospital where she was treated for inflammation of the brain, before being released to recover at her theme park home.

Mary received around-the-clock care while recovering at Paradise Country. (Supplied: Paradise Country)

Today, nearly three months after returning to the park, Mary was released into her outdoor enclosure.

"I'm a little bit emotional when I think back at how many months it took to get her here," the park's wildlife curator, Lauren Mousley, said.

" It took a lot of dedication, hard work, happy tears and sad tears, but it's a great day … and we believe she's ready for it. "

After her escape, Queensland's Department of Primary Industries (DPI) conducted an onsite investigation of Mary's enclosure and the wider facilities at Paradise Country.

"[DPI] is satisfied the enclosures were already compliant with legislated requirements," animal security general manager Allison Crook said at the time.

Ms Mousley said while the enclosure was found to be compliant, several new measures had been introduced to Mary's habitat to prevent another "abnormally large leap" and a second escape.

Signs have been installed welcoming Mary back to her enclosure on the Gold Coast. (ABC News: Glenn Mullane)

She said the ledges overlooking the enclosure were now "domed" to prevent any animals from getting a toe-hold.

"We've also re-landscaped the habitat space so that all the trees are nice and central," she said.

"We had to put some other guards in, some non-climbable material on the trees, because they are climbers by nature, but we've extended those and increased the number of guards we have as well."

Mary is expected to be reintroduced to her fellow devil, Mavka, in the coming weeks.

title: School holidays flight disruption fear as QantasLink staff threaten action
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Qantas is at the Fair Work Commission trying to prevent the Transport Workers Union (TWU) from going ahead with industrial action next week.

The planned 24-hour strike action on Thursday relates to QantasLink flights out of Sydney and freight services but may affect those travelling to selected regional areas.

School holidays are about to begin in Queensland, Victoria and the Northern Territory.

The industrial action involves about 650 employees, with most working on Qantas Freight and a smaller proportion servicing QantasLink flights at Sydney Airport.

These workers do not service Qantas mainline and international services, or QantasLink at any other airport.

Qantas said it had developed contingency plans to minimise any impact on QantasLink customers and operations, if industrial action went ahead.

"We remain committed to reaching an agreement with our Qantas Ground Services employees that includes annual pay rises for our people," it said in a statement.

Transport Workers Union national secretary Michael Kaine said workers were not taking the action lightly.

"Any disruption to freight, including Australia Post shipments, sits solely at the feet of Qantas management and its brutal disregard for customers and the workforce," Mr Kaine said.

In a statement, Australia Post said should industrial action occur, it had "detailed contingency plans in place" and would work closely with freight partners to minimise any impact on customers and delivery services.

Transport Workers' Union national secretary Michael Kaine. (AAP: Lukas Coch)

Mr Kaine blamed increasing casualisation and insecure work for the ground crew for contributing to "shocking safety failures", something Qantas disputes.

"This action comes just over a year after a Qantas Freight worker was tragically killed on Father's Day, " he said.

Qantas disputes TWU claims that safety incidents have increased since ground handling moved to Swissport more than five years ago.

Mr Kaine claims Qantas is continuing to "splinter" its workforce to suppress wages and "smash conditions".

"This is corporate greed on steroids, and it comes at the expense of quality service for customers, and safe, reliable jobs for the workforce."

Qantas ground staff vote for strike The Transport Workers Union says 97 per cent of 350 workers who voted backed industrial action, including work stoppages ranging from one to 24 hours.

Qantas said discussions through the Fair Work Commission had been constructive and negotiations were continuing.

title: K'gari resort set to be sold to US travel giant
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Traditional owners of K'gari, formerly Fraser Island, say they are hoping to work with the American company buying the island's largest hotel.

Kingfisher Bay Resort, which has 269 rooms, villas and holiday houses, is one of about 15 tourism operations being sold by Kelsian Group to tourism company Journey Beyond.

Lake McKenzie (Boorangoora) is one of K'gari's most popular destinations. (ABC Wide Bay: Johanna Marie)

Private equity firm Crestview Partners, based in the United States, owns Journey Beyond and already operates several high-profile tourism sites, including the Ghan and Indian Pacific railways, along with the Ayers Rock Resort.

The $145.8 million cash sale pays for Kelsian's tourism portfolio, which also includes K'gari Beach Resort and the K'gari Explorer tour operation.

Kingfisher Bay Resort offers 4WD tours to explore the world heritage-listed island. (ABC Wide Bay: Johanna Marie)

Sydney Harbour's Captain Cook Cruises, along with Kelsian's ferry and coach services, also form part of the deal.

The Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) approved the sale in a determination last week, finding the deal was unlikely to affect competition in any market.

Kelsian Group announced on Thursday the Foreign Investment Review Board had approved the sale, and the company was working towards signing over contracts and authorisations to Journey Beyond.

Traditional owners positive

The Butchulla people are K'gari's traditional owners, receiving native title rights over the island in 2014.

Butchulla Native Title Aboriginal Corporation chair Shawn Wondunna-Foley said the group welcomed any new owners or investors to the island, provided they worked constructively with traditional owners.

Fraser Island was officially renamed K'gari following a Butchulla ceremony in 2023. (ABC Wide Bay: Pat Heagney)

"Our focus is not on where investors come from, but on how they conduct themselves on Country," he said.

"We look forward to engaging with the new owners and exploring opportunities that can deliver lasting social, cultural, environmental and economic benefits for both the Butchulla people and the wider community."

Professor Daniel Gschwind from the Griffith University Institute for Tourism said international visitors expected to see genuine engagement with First Nations people in their tourism destinations.

"I would certainly encourage the new owners to build very strongly on what is ultimately a competitive advantage to be located in such an iconic, not just natural location, but also important First Nations destination," he said.

Daniel Gschwind is a Professor of Practice at the Griffith Institute for Tourism. (ABC News: Chris Gillette)

Kelsian Group and Journey Beyond did not respond to requests for comment.

Experiential tourism

When the sale agreement was first announced, Journey Beyond CEO Chris Tallent said the additional operations would work alongside its existing brands.

"They create new opportunities for guests to seamlessly extend their journeys across Australia — whether that's transitioning from rail to reef, river to resort, or city to sea," he said in February.

Journey Beyond acquired The Ayers Rock Resort in February. (Instagram: Explore Uluru)

Professor Gschwind said the resort was closely aligned with Journey Beyond's strategy of offering "experiential tourism".

"People don't want to just enjoy infrastructure and hotel rooms," he said.

"They want to really walk away from a tourism experience with … something that they can emotionally connect with, something they can talk about, something they can put on Instagram, something that they can brag about."

Kelsian Group chief executive Graeme Leigh told an August earnings call he expected the deal to be completed by the end of the year.

title: Outback nurse credits non-profit counselling service for saving career
text:
Tell us about your experience.

An outback nurse who has worked across remote parts of Australia says a peer-to-peer counselling service for nurses and midwives was a "godsend" during the most difficult time of his life.

Remote area nurse Dave Corstorphan previously worked in the Pilbara and Kimberley in Western Australia's north, including in the state's northernmost community Kalumburu.

Mr Corstorphan said he almost left the profession due to work stress and following the death of his wife.

However, he credits the free peer counselling service Midwife Health Program Victoria (NMHPV) for providing crucial support.

"I accessed that service, and it was an absolute godsend," Mr Corstorphan said.

" I would have just walked away completely from it [the job]. "

Mr Corstorphan said speaking directly to a counsellor who had been a nurse or midwife themselves was a game changer.

"The fact they've worked the shift work, done time in hospitals, know the conditions you're working under and seen all that, it makes a big, big difference," he said.

"You can say, 'This is what is happening,' and they go, 'Yep, I understand.'"

Dave Corstorphan says nursing in remote and regional health facilities is not without its challenges, especially for new nurses. (Supplied: Dave Corstorphan)

Up to 60 consults a month

Due to its success in Victoria, the Nurse and Midwife Program was extended across the country in 2024.

The Nurse Midwife Health Program Australia (NMHPA) runs as an independent and not-for-profit service, funded by the Commonwealth government as opposed to being led by state and territory governments.

NMHPA chief executive officer Lori-Anne Sharp and midwife Martine Kilday visited the Kimberley in August.

They said 42 per cent of staff who asked for help worked in regional locations.

Ms Sharp said counsellors received up to 60 calls a month from midwives, nurses and students.

Lori-Anne Sharp and Martine Kilday say burnout, shift work, and isolation are common issues for nurses and midwives. (ABC Kimberley: Esse Deves)

"The community really values the work they do, but they also need to be supported in the challenges of the work," she said.

"The shift work is another layer of that for rural and remote [workers]; it can be the large stints, long days, consecutive days."

An evaluation report into NMHPA's impact found the top five challenges raised by employees were anxiety and depression, stress, psychological distress, occupational violence, bullying or harassment, and burnout.

Ms Kilday said many staff were not aware of the service.

"Nurses and midwives are very good at looking after others … they tend to put themselves last on the list of self-care," she said.

Mr Corstrophan encouraged his regional and remote colleagues — some of whom were the only nurse in a specific location — to seek help.

"I think there is this fear of weakness, appearing weak, that we need to be stoic the whole time, particularly for our patients," he said.

WA Country Health Services says it employs about 4,200 nurses and midwives across regional areas. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

"The work can be quite confronting."

Culture shock

Mr Corstorphan said nursing in remote and regional health facilities was not without its challenges, especially for new nurses.

He said a perceived lack of support, burnout and feelings of isolation were common outside metropolitan areas.

"They are full of energy to start with and they burn out very fast," Mr Corstorphan said.

"The people who live out there have always lived with what's out there and are very accepting, but for a lot of nurses from the cities, it's a culture shock."

'Heart of healthcare'

Both Mr Corstorphan and NMHPA said many staff may be cautious about raising their concerns while working within a state government department.

According to WA's Country Health Service, there are more than 4,200 nurses and approximately 240 midwives working across the state's regional health facilities.

More than 240 midwives are employed with the WA Country Health Service. (ABC North Queensland: Nathalie Fernbach)

WACHS nursing and midwifery executive director Alison Weatherstone said supporting the workforce was important, while acknowledging the "rewarding" and "demanding" work.

"Staff have access to confidential counselling through our Employee Assistance Program, as well as debriefing and peer support following stressful or challenging events," she said.

"We also provide targeted programs for particular teams, including specialist support through our 24/7 Command Centre and reflective supervision for cancer services staff.

"Nurses and midwives are at the heart of healthcare in country WA."

title: Fiji declares national HIV emergency as cases soar
text:
Tell us about your experience.

Fiji has declared a national HIV emergency, with new statistics showing one in 60 adults are living with the virus.

The government said in a statement posted on Facebook that 2,016 people were diagnosed with HIV in 2025, representing a 27 per cent increase in positive cases from the previous year.

Fifty-nine babies were born with HIV last year, and 18 died before their first birthday, it also said.

Authorities said expanded testing had helped uncover infections, enabling earlier treatment.

Fiji now plans to widen access to free, voluntary and confidential testing, preventive medicines, as well as harm-reduction services for injecting drug users and treatment.

Five years ago one in 167 people in Fiji had the virus.

HIV testing is being rapidly expanded across Fiji. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter, file)

Chair of Fiji's National HIV Outbreak Response, Jason Mitchell, told ABC's The World that there had been a scarcity of needles in Fiji because of law enforcement operations.

He said those operations were appropriate, but had hindered harm reduction efforts.

"We need to make needles and syringes widely available to the public, where anyone who is actually injecting has access to sterile needles and syringes so they can avoid sharing," Mr Mitchell said.

"I think it shows real bravery and real leadership of our government to introduce this and introduce it very quickly and scale it up."

He predicted it would take "upwards of five years" to bring the epidemic under control.

"The complexities of our communities that are impacted by HIV and engaging with them and working with them makes it very difficult for us to turn an epidemic like this around," he said.

"With the country rising together, we will get on top of this; it will just take time."

Fiji, a country of about 900,000 people, is experiencing one of the world's sharpest rises in new infections, according to UNAIDS.

It estimates that 9,100 Fijians were living with HIV last year, that only 39 per cent knew their status, and that 22 per cent were receiving antiretroviral treatment.

"Fiji has recognised the urgency of the moment and is stepping up its response," UNAIDS executive director Winnie Byanyima said.

" It is also a stark reminder to the world that AIDS is not over. "

Among cases with a known transmission route, more than half were linked to sexual transmission and over 42 per cent to injecting drugs, UNAIDS said.

The agency welcomed government plans for a needle and syringe program and expanded access to pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP), medicine used to lower the risk of contracting HIV.

The government has set up a five-minister cabinet subcommittee to remove barriers to action.

It said discrimination against people living with HIV was illegal and services were available nationwide.

Fiji's estimate of one in 60 adults living with HIV remains below parts of Africa, where nearly one in 35 adults are living with HIV, according to the World Health Organization.

title: Flooded market leaves pioneering WA abalone ranch close to the end
text:
Tell us about your experience.

The world's first ocean-ranched abalone operation is winding down on Western Australia's southern coast as export prices fall and losses rise.

In 2019, the business was riding high on an export "gold rush" to Chinese consumers, making it the biggest employer in Augusta.

Locals were employed to dive and harvest abalone off artificial reefs in Flinders Bay, as well as process the molluscs at a nearby facility.

Now, Rare Foods Australia (RFA) is winding down the business, having accumulated losses of more than $25 million as of June last year, according to financial documents.

The molluscs are considered a delicacy in a number of Asian countries. (ABC News: Nicholas Martyr)

The company's financial hardship comes amid a slump in the global abalone market, driven by drastically expanded supply from China's farmed abalone industry.

The company's 2024–25 financial report, lodged with the corporate regulator earlier this month, shows RFA sustained a yearly loss of $4,833,469, and that its net assets had halved from $9.6 million to $4.7 million.

A wind-down strategy adopted in 2025 included workforce restructuring and reductions in operating expenditure.

By June, it had delisted from the Australian Securities Exchange to "reduce the significant costs associated with ASX listing".

The company also stopped seeding juvenile abalone into its artificial reefs in Augusta.

RFA declined ABC's request for comment.

Family founder leaves industry

After founding the company, then known as Ocean Grown Abalone in 2011, long-time managing director Brad Adams left RFA and the wider seafood industry earlier this year.

Having followed his father's footsteps into the industry, he said stiff competition from Chinese producers had effectively halved export prices for greenlip abalone.

Brad Adams says adapting to changed conditions is essential, but not always possible. (ABC South West WA: Jon Daly)

"We were probably averaging around $55 to $60 a kilogram. Ranched abalone is now around $30, $35," Mr Adams said.

"Any business that loses half its margin that quickly has to respond and adapt pretty quickly.

"Sometimes you can't adapt, and you just have to look for other opportunities, and that's not the end of the world either."

Aquaculture output 'halved'

A drastic expansion over two decades has seen the Chinese industry reach production of around 200,000 tonnes per year.

The result has been a flooded Chinese market, once the biggest consumer of Australian abalone.

Mr Adams said other big players were also exiting Australia's aquaculture industry.

"It's probably halved production in the last two years," he said.

Last year, two Tasmanian farms closed, including an operation at Bicheno owned by Yumbah Aquaculture, Australia's largest producer.

Yumbah Aquaculture's Kangaroo Island facility, which has operated for more than 30 years. (Supplied: Yumbah Aquaculture)

The devastating algal bloom along South Australia's coast also saw Yumbah close its farm on Kangaroo Island.

The challenging conditions have also halted plans for the industry to establish another foothold along WA's southern coast near Esperance.

A proposal for an abalone ranch and broader aquaculture precinct began in 2017, backed by the Esperance Tjaltjraak Native Title Aboriginal Corporation [ETNTAC], in collaboration with Rare Foods Australia and Yumbah.

But the project has sat on the shelf since.

ETNTAC chief executive Peter Bednall said it made sense to investigate the project's future potential, but the recent downturn meant further expansion was in question.

Peter Bednall says more needs to be done to build community resilience in small towns reliant on international industry. (ABC News: Emily Smith)

"The reality is the concept we explored needs an awful lot of capital," he said.

"We think that's really important for towns like this, that our young people have the opportunities to stay here and develop their expertise in a range of different areas."

title: Minister dodges migration modelling question eight times amid farmers’ fury
text:

Employment Minister Amanda Rishworth has repeatedly failed to say whether Labor modelled the impacts of its new migration plan on wages or the broader economy, despite the government claiming plans proposed by One Nation and the Coalition would damage the Australian economy. Speaking on radio on Friday morning, Rishworth was asked eight times whether the government had modelled the impact on wages of significant cuts to backpacker visas, and the broader economic impact of Labor’s plan, and eight times did not give a direct answer. Employment and Industrial Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth. Dominic Lorrimer In response to repeated questions, Rishworth said she was “not really able to comment” on the modelling, later saying it was a matter for Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke. As minister for both employment and workplace relations, Rishworth has oversight over workers’ wages and is a member of cabinet. Labor has vowed to cut nearly 40,000 backpacker visas per year and crack down on overstayers through increased enforcement as part of a plan that Burke unveiled on Thursday. The Coalition and the National Farmers’ Federation have slammed the overhaul, arguing it will raise the price of food and hurt primary producers.

Advertisement

The new regulations do not lower Labor’s current net overseas migration target, but instead aim to help the government achieve its plan of 245,000 migrants by June next year and then 225,000 by mid-2028. One Nation wants negative migration, followed by an annual net migration figure of 130,000, while the Coalition wants a figure slightly lower than 170,000. One Nation’s plan has been widely condemned as economically reckless. Related Article Immigration What are Labor’s new migration rules for Australia? Net overseas migration is the total number of people entering the country minus the number of people leaving. During her ABC Radio National appearance, Rishworth said the policy amounted to “important and sensible changes” that contributed to a “sustainable” migration policy. Rishworth was unable to say whether there would be a positive impact to domestic workers’ wages or increased wage bills for farmers. Asked a third time about the modelling of wages, Rishworth said: “We always want to see decent wages for workers, but there is a safety net in this country, and if the suggestion is suggesting somehow that backpackers are getting paid under that safety net, then I would find that unacceptable.”

Opposition employment spokeswoman Jane Hume told this masthead that Labor wasn’t serious about lowering migration, and Rishworth had proven it. “Amanda Rishworth is the employment minister, yet she can’t answer a basic question about the impact of her government’s own policy on Australian wages,” Hume said. “If she hasn’t seen the modelling, she should. If it doesn’t exist, Labor should say so. Under Labor’s plan, working holidaymakers or backpackers will face a ballot system to access second- and third-year visa renewals. Kyalite Pistachios general manager Ben Seton-Stewart said his orchard operation was highly dependent on access to a reliable seasonal workforce. title: Why I hate ‘top 100’ book lists (and can’t stop reading them)
text:
What is it about these Top 100 book lists? They are absurd. If critics choose them, they reflect only the critics’ tastes. If chosen by the public, they reflect only what people interested in voting have read and liked. You can’t say these are the best books of all time; you can only say they represent something about readers’ choices at a particular moment.

And yet like many others, I find these lists compulsive reading. I want to see if my favourites are on it, or if a book I hate is high on the list. Then I moan and groan and avidly wait for the next list to appear.

I find these book ranking lists compulsive reading. Getty Images/iStockphoto

The latest poll is from an ABC Radio National drive to find the 100 best Australian books of all time. This is a welcome antidote to international lists, which heavily favour American and British titles and rarely mention Australian books. You can nominate a shortlist of up to 10 books by October 1 and the final list will be announced live on a countdown on October 17 and 18.

I wonder what book will be number one? Possibly a Winton or a Garner or a Dalton or a Zusak – a book by a contemporary writer because these are the books most people read. Patrick White, long regarded as Australia’s best writer, is out of fashion. And whether we like it or not, fashion rules these lists.

title: Decked out: How card games shuffled the everyday language of sports
text:
As a card-carrying member of the word nerd club, I can report that English has long been hooked on card games. Whether we hold the upper hand, pass the buck or offer a bargaining chip, our deck is stacked with table talk. Stacked in spades, with recent years only upping the ante.

Blame Trump, I guess. But that’s too simple a game, though trump (the verb) is Exhibit A, a corruption of triumph. Or triomphe in fact, a la the Parisian arch. A popular trick-taking game, triomphe is the forebear of euchre. The pastime fostered the idea of a trump card being your winning edge, the deal-clincher. Grand as that sounds, I love how NZ slang during WWI called anyone in authority, typically a cocky middle manager, as trump of the dump.

The English language has long been hooked on card games. iStock

Staying with US politics, Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal offered a clean slate of social and economic reforms where tax revenue was above board – a further card-game borrowing. Despite that, any new deal will leave some citizens in the lurch, a phrase from cribbage. Lurch refers to an emphatic win where you “street” your opponent by more than twice their score. (Bear in mind that street is the column of peg-holes on a cribbage board, and nothing to do with Pennsylvania Avenue.) As for lurch, dictionary sleuth Michael Quinion suspects “lurz werden” to be the source, the German phrase meaning to become short.

At the stadium, table games and sport also meld, another verb drawn from the pack, canasta this time. In tennis, the US Open wraps the calendar of grand slams – a term via the bridge club. Just as we’re entering showdown season in football. And yes, showdown is another casino legacy. Poker on this occasion, when all the bluff and bluster is done, the stakes are high, demanding all players to lay down their hands, the showdown a sort of facing up.

title: The forces turning Australia's inflation fears into a reality
text:
In brief Reserve Bank governor Michele Bullock said "upside risks to inflation appear to be materialising".

It reaffirmed expectations that the board would hike rates again at this month's meeting.

The Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) fears about inflation have materialised, its governor Michele Bullock says, which could force it to raise interest rates again.

Her comments during a parliamentary hearing on Friday morning reaffirmed expectations that the central bank would hike rates for a fourth time this year at its upcoming board meeting in late September.

Inflation was too high, but the key question for the RBA at that meeting would be whether the bank's three rate rises to date were enough to bring inflation back to target in a reasonable time, Bullock said.

At its last meeting in August, the RBA forecast that inflation would return to the middle of its target range of 2-3 per cent by the end of 2027.

Even that was not assured, with inflation more likely to overshoot the bank's forecasts than undershoot it.

If that proved to be the case, more rate hikes might be warranted, the RBA board said at the time.

"Developments since then suggest that, although growth in the Australian economy is slowing, some of these upside risks to inflation appear to be materialising," Bullock said on Friday.

The Middle East conflict, the AI boom, and extreme weather events have added to pressure on energy, food, and tech prices, she said.

"There is little sign of resolution in the Middle East conflict. Oil and related prices have increased sharply again and will add directly to inflation."

The benchmark Brent crude price remained above US$104 ($146) a barrel, despite a modest sell-off in oil overnight on news that Saudi Arabia plans to bring its East-West pipeline back online in a reduced capacity following attacks by Iran-backed Houthi forces.

But as businesses increasingly saw no end in sight to the war and price increases, they were growing more inclined to pass on costs to consumers, which risked making inflation more persistent, Bullock said.

After inflation came in hotter than expected in July, money markets have raised the chance for a September rate rise above 80 per cent, with two hikes fully priced in by March.

Higher-for-longer interest rates and fuel prices would hit economic growth, but that has been swamped by the AI boom, which has pushed up demand in a way the RBA did not foresee.

"Just back from the US and in addition to ... the upside risk of inflation from the Middle East, what is also very striking is how strong the AI and tech boom is and has been," RBA deputy governor Andrew Hauser said.

"That's not just true in the US; it's true in the Asia Pacific region as well, who are of course our closest trading partners, and our forecasts for global growth have been repeatedly surprised on the upside."

Given Australia's productivity malaise, a period of slower growth was needed to bring inflation down, Bullock said.

The nation's deepening housing downturn would help take some steam out of the economy, but while prices have fallen in most capital cities, they remain about 50 per cent higher than in early 2020.

title: 'I am learning': HYROX athlete apologises and withdraws after viral defecation incident
text:
In Brief Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk has issued an apology after soiling herself during a HYROX race in Beijing.

The incident prompted HYROX to formally change its rulebook to withdraw racers if their faeces pose a "contamination risk".

The Australian athlete at the centre of the HYROX defecation controversy has apologised and retroactively withdrawn from the race after footage of the incident went viral internationally.

Social media footage showed Australian athlete Joanna Wietrzyk, who holds the women's HYROX solo pro world record, competing at exercise stations with faeces on her legs during a race in Beijing over the weekend.

She finished the race and won despite the incident.

In a statement posted to Instagram on Thursday night, Wietrzyk apologised for her decision to continue competing.

"I want to offer my sincere apology to the people of China, my fellow competitors, the spectators and the HYROX organizers for what happened during the race in Beijing," she wrote.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"I felt completely fit and healthy at the start of the race, with no reason to expect any illness. Looking back, I regret the decision to not have stepped off the track.

"I recognize that I should have made a different choice. I take responsibility for my decision to continue and am deeply sorry for the discomfort and disruption it caused."

Wietrzyk also announced that she would forfeit the points she earned as the competition winner.

"I am learning from this experience and will carry those lessons with me, including remembering that there is more to life than racing and knowing when it is right to step away," she said.

"On reflection, I have decided to retroactively withdraw from the race and forfeit the points I earned."

Ending her statement, Wietrzyk said: "Thank you to those standing by me, both as an athlete and as a person, during this time, and to everyone who has reached out with kindness and support.

"It means more to me than I can properly express right now. I will be taking some time to recover, reflect and look after myself and my family away from the noise."

Days of silence following controversy

The Instagram statement came almost a week after the incident.

HYROX is a fitness and endurance race that combines 8km of running with exercises such as rowing, sled pushes and wall balls, carried out in indoor exhibition halls.

Wietrzyk initially shared a selfie on her Instagram story after the race, which showed her lying down with an intravenous line in her arm. It was captioned: "Go hard or go home they say ... a win is a win".

Multiple media outlets also reported that Wietrzyk's major sponsor, Puma, was distancing itself from the athlete after their collaborative line appeared to be quietly removed from the sportswear giant's website a day ago.

The page has since been restored online, with a Puma spokesperson telling CBC News that some landing pages were "unintentionally taken offline".

Incident prompts HYROX rule change

The incident has prompted backlash and criticism of HYROX's health and safety standards, with many wondering why Wietrzyk was permitted to continue competing with fecal matter visibly running down her legs.

HYROX co-founder Moritz Fürste issued a statement earlier this week apologising to those "directly or indirectly" affected by the incident, "as well as to everyone who felt we did not handle the situation like we should have".

"HYROX made a mistake by not reacting immediately to the incident," Fürste said. "In the end it is my job to foresee these potential incidents — and I did not."

Fürste said event processes have since been improved, including "rulebook changes" and "new rules and procedures" that he said will "prevent situations like this from happening again".

"We learn and try to get better everyday," he said.

In the updated HYROX rulebook, a racer can be withdrawn on medical grounds if their "blood, vomit, urine, or faeces poses a welfare or contamination risk to the racer or to other racers … in line with HYROX’s medical and hygiene SOPs".

Gut issues and endurance sports

According to research by Monash University, strenuous exercise lasting two hours or more — particularly running — appears to exacerbate gut disturbances.

Researchers estimate 30 to 70 per cent of athletes experience gastrointestinal symptoms, with endurance athletes particularly susceptible.

Bec Hoschke, a former professional triathlete and Ironman champion who now coaches endurance athletes in Sydney, told SBS News earlier this week that gut health can be a "highly sensitive thing for many endurance athletes".

She said the HYROX incident was a "very difficult situation" for the parties involved: the competition, the athlete and her competitors.

"Athletes make enormous sacrifices for international competition," she said. "For some athletes, it's their living."

She said the issue was not only one of public health and hygiene but also of the health and well-being of the athlete involved.

"I can't imagine the mental impact all of this is having on someone. I think she's only in her early 20s as well. It's enormously confronting for someone to have to deal with at that age."

Australia and New Zealand could follow in Canada's footsteps to become "associate members" of the European Union, a top EU official has suggested.

title: Does the sight of small holes make you feel ill? There's a reason for that
text:
Imagine you’re scrolling through TikTok and come across an image of a lotus seed pod or sponge.

You might not think much about it, but some people instantly feel sick. Their skin crawls, they feel nauseous, disgusted or very uncomfortable, and quickly swipe away.

The object is harmless. So why does it trigger such a strong reaction?

This reaction is known as trypophobia, an aversion to clusters of holes or circular patterns.

About one in six people have at least some degree of discomfort when seeing these patterns.

What is trypophobia?

Despite the "phobia" in its name, trypophobia is not simply a "fear of holes". It is also not recognised as a standalone mental health disorder. Unlike many phobias, disgust (rather than fear) is often the more dominant emotion.

Common triggers are lotus seed pods and honeycomb, or even everyday objects such as sponges, crumpets, bubbles, aerated chocolate or strawberries.

For most people with trypophobia these reactions are mild and can include disgust, nausea, skin crawling sensation, fear and anxiety.

But for a small group, symptoms can become so distressing they lead to people avoiding particular images, objects, or situations. This is a level of avoidance usually seen in specific phobias, such as arachnophobia, a fear of spiders.

In my own research, some participants avoided strawberries, cooking or baking, clothing, and even showers because of trypophobia-related triggers. These examples show trypophobia can sometimes significantly affect a person’s life.

Why is trypophobia having a moment?

The short answer is social media. Media stories, TikTok videos and online communities helped make trypophobia mainstream.

Shared images are often digitally altered to maximise discomfort and provoke strong reactions.

Research also suggests social media might influence how people experience trypophobia. For instance, in one 2024 study, almost two-thirds of people heard about it through social media. Those who had previously heard of trypophobia reported stronger reactions than those who had not.

But that doesn’t mean social media created trypophobia. Around one-quarter of people with trypophobia in the same study had never heard of it. Social media might increase awareness, but it cannot explain why some people react so strongly in the first place.

Why do some people react this way?

Scientists still debate why trypophobia exists, with two leading explanations emerging.

The first is the threat-detection theory. Some researchers argue trypophobic images resemble patterns found on poisonous or dangerous animals, such as snakes. According to this theory, humans might have evolved to react negatively to these visual cues because they can signal danger.

The second theory focuses on avoiding disease, with support from increasing evidence. Clusters of holes can look like skin lesions, rashes, parasites or signs of infection. Although lotus seed pods or honeycomb are completely harmless, the visual resemblance might activate psychological systems that evolved to help us avoid contamination and disease.

Both theories suggest trypophobic patterns might resemble things that historically posed a threat to human health or survival. In other words, the holes themselves might not be the problem. Instead, the brain might interpret these patterns as signs of a biological threat.

What people react to is not the object itself, but what the brain subconsciously thinks the pattern might represent. This might explain why harmless objects can trigger reactions that seem far stronger than the situation warrants.

Does it need treatment?

Fortunately, most people only have mild symptoms and do not need treatment. Understanding that trypophobia is a recognised and common phenomenon can often be reassuring.

However, if symptoms cause significant distress or begin to interfere with daily life, it might be worth seeking professional support.

Even though trypophobia is often associated with disgust, many people also experience fear and anxiety. So treatments used for specific phobias, particularly exposure-based approaches, might be helpful.

This might involve gradually and safely confronting feared or uncomfortable images, situations or sensations while reducing avoidance. Over time, people learn they can tolerate their distress and that the anticipated harm does not occur.

Until recently, no treatment had been specifically tested for trypophobia. However, a recently published study I co-authored found a single intensive treatment session targeting fear and disgust reduced symptoms and helped participants engage more fully in daily activities.

The bottom line

Trypophobia is more than an internet meme. It is a genuine psychological experience that can range from mild discomfort to significant distress.

Growing evidence suggests these patterns might activate ancient psychological systems designed to detect danger, contamination and disease. The brain could be responding as if it has detected a threat, even when there is no threat.

For most people, reactions are brief. But if not, support is available. Ask your GP for a referral to a psychologist.

title: Burke's pitch to worried farmers as he warns of migration overhaul risk
text:
IN BRIEF The home affairs minister says there will be impacts on industry from the migration changes.

He also suggested farmers should consider hiring Pacific workers amid concerns over backpacker labour shortages.

The Home Affairs Department has engineered a slowdown in backpacker visas to reduce arrivals and is now urging farmers to consider hiring Pacific workers to pick their crops.

The National Farmers' Federation has led a campaign to axe visa bottlenecks amid growing industry anxiety that fruits and other crops will wither on trees without the labour force needed to harvest them.

The agricultural sector is warning the shortages will increase supermarket prices.

As the federal government moves to reduce arrivals to Australia, its visa overhaul includes introducing a ballot system for backpackers hoping to spend more than one year in Australia on a working holiday visa.

It will also cut the available long-term visas. Backpackers from the United Kingdom will be exempt from the requirements because of the UK's free trade deal with Australia.
