Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

In an interview with SBS News, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has encouraged any horticulture businesses struggling to secure harvest workers to consider the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme and Pacific workers.

"Our preferred agriculture visa has always been the PALM scheme, the Pacific workers visa. When I was employment minister, we did a lot to improve the rules to avoid worker exploitation on the Pacific, on the PALM visa," he said.

"At the time that we were improving those rules, we had some of the farm organisations say to us, 'If you do this, our members will just go and use backpackers.'"

He maintains there is a Pacific workforce ready to step in.

"Now, if the reason that people are more reliant on backpackers and refusing to use Pacific workers is because they're upset that we've ended exploitation in those areas, I think that is a very different question for a number of operators.

"That doesn't depict the whole of the farm sector, not for a minute, and a whole lot of them still use the Pacific Labour Scheme, but the Pacific Labour Scheme right now has extra capacity. Those extra workers are available."

'I can't quarantine any sector of Australia'

Burke said he can't quarantine any sector of the economy from the impacts of the migration shake-up.

The government wants to reduce the number of working holidaymakers, crack down on visa overstayers and tighten allowances for international students as part of its push to reduce migration numbers.

Farmers and the Nationals have been among the critics of changes set to affect backpackers, who the former rely on to pick fruit in the regions.

Only 45,000 working holiday-makers will be able to stay in Australia for a second year under the system, and only 5,000 for a third year — down from 57,000 and 31,000 respectively.

Burke told SBS News there will be challenges for industry to adjust to the changes.

"No matter what you do, if you are lowering (immigration) numbers, there are challenges across the visa system and across the Australian economy," he said.

"I can't quarantine any sector of Australia. What I can do is make sure —as numbers are lowered, and they need to be lowered because of the challenges we have with housing supply — I want the rest of the economy to have the softest landing possible."

One in five international students to be impacted

The government's plan to stop some international students from bringing their families to Australia could affect about one in five people, amid warnings of an economic hit if some choose to study elsewhere.

International students and those on graduate visas will no longer be able to bring family members with them to Australia under the reforms.

PhD students and some Pacific and ASEAN students are exempt from the proposal.

Burke told SBS News around 19 per cent of the cohort bring in family members to Australia. It's unclear whether that includes PhD students, who are more likely to bring family than undergraduates.

"International students tend to be younger, and so family obligations are a very different issue," Burke said.

Asked whether the proposal, which could affect 19 per cent of the cohort, would amount to a major revenue hit for universities and the economy, Burke insisted demand for student spots will bridge any gap.

"It's actually not, for the very simple reason that at the moment, we have more students wanting to study in Australia than we have places," he said.

"Whereas for skilled workers, everyone who an employer can find, they take, because that's completely demand-driven. There's no planning level on temporary skilled visas at all.

"You don't have the same impact for students, nor do you have the same size of demand simply because people tend to be younger."

There are around 680,582 international students in Australia. About 295,000 new international students are due to commence next year, in student cap figures unchanged from this year.

Universities Australia welcomed the carve-out for PhD students, saying Australia was competing globally for researchers and highly-skilled people.

The Group of Eight representing Australia's research-intensive universities said it educated about half of PhD students — about 12,000, with half of those requiring secondary visas for dependants.

"Most of our undergraduate international students are quite young. They're ... 18, 19, 20, and many of them aren't coming here with their parents, frankly," CEO Vicki Thompson told ABC News.

Other measures that will affect students include preventing so-called 'visa hopping', with a new qualification scale to allow only foreign students transferring to higher-level courses (bachelor's to master's, for example) to extend their visas.

title: 'A struggle every day': There's a hidden side to Australia's student visa debate
text:
IN BRIEF The government says the changes will help cut net overseas migration to 245,000 this financial year.

Students and migration experts have raised concerns about how some of the new restrictions could affect migrants.

For almost nine years, Bashshar Khalid has been building a life in Australia.

He arrived as an international student in 2017, completed a three-year bachelor's degree in business and then a two-year master's degree before entering the workforce.

But graduating was only the beginning.

Khalid first moved onto a temporary graduate visa, known as a subclass 485, and recently secured a subclass 482 work visa after finding employment in sales.

He told SBS News that making the transition from international student to skilled worker was far from straightforward.

One of the biggest difficulties was convincing an employer to invest in someone whose ability to remain in Australia had an expiry date attached to it.

"We basically have to work twice as hard, or we just have to prove our skill set to our employers," he said.

At one point, Khalid's temporary graduate visa was approaching expiry while his employer-sponsored visa application was still being processed.

He moved onto a bridging visa while he waited for an outcome.

"Every day when you wake up, or every day you're going into the office to work, you're not sure whether the application will be approved or not ... It's basically a struggle every day."

Bashshar Khalid came to Australia as an international student in 2017 and recently secured a 482 work visa. Credit: Image: Supplied

Government's migration crackdown

Now, the federal government has announced another suite of changes aimed at tightening Australia's migration system and further reducing net overseas migration (NOM).

The changes include measures targeting so-called "visa hopping", restrictions on secondary applicants on most student visas and stronger measures to ensure people without valid visas leave Australia.

The government will also introduce a 'no further stay' condition on all visitor visas and crack down on migration agents it says knowingly support applications without merit.

Announcing the reforms on Thursday, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said the government was targeting people who would "never" meet the requirements for permanent residency but continued moving through the migration system to extend their stay.

"They effectively jump from visa to visa, use the appeals process to be able to stay here as long as possible until it eventually becomes absurd to not just let them stay," he said.

Critics say the crackdown could limit legitimate study and work opportunities.

Khalid said he believes there should be a clearer distinction between people switching courses simply to stay in the country, and migrants legitimately progressing through study and skilled employment.

"We have contributed to the economy. We have paid our taxes. We have done everything right by the book," he said.

"There couldn't be one single hard and fast rule about everything.

"If they could genuinely prove that the change of career is more of a personal choice and not just for a visa hopping case, then I think they should be given a fair chance."

Former immigration department deputy secretary Abul Rizvi also supports reducing visa hopping but cautioned against applying restrictions too broadly.

"As a general rule, I think reducing visa hopping is a good idea," he said.

READ MORE Tony Burke set to unveil Labor's new migration plan amid working holiday visa concerns

"The question will be how broadly those measures are applied, because if they're applied too broadly, there will be unintended consequences."

Rizvi pointed to businesses that bring workers into Australia on business visas when they urgently need their skills while waiting for a skilled temporary visa to be processed.

If those transitions are restricted while skilled visa processing times remain lengthy, he said, businesses could face difficulties.

'It would have definitely affected my decision'

For Khalid, the uncertainty of Australia's migration system has already made planning a career difficult.

Khalid said policy changes could mean migrants made significant decisions based on one set of rules, only to find the pathway had shifted.

"If my pathway was not as clear ... it would have been a major decision for me whether I should stay on in the country or leave the country," he said.

Had the pathway been more restrictive when he was studying, Khalid said it "would have definitely affected" his decision.

His recently granted 482 visa now provides a potential pathway towards permanent residency.

"After spending a good amount of time in this country, you sort of feel like it's your second home," he said.

What will the changes mean for students with families?

The government's reforms also restrict secondary applicants on most student visas, potentially affecting students seeking to have family members join them in Australia.

Muath Alqarni, a Saudi master's degree student at the University of Melbourne, told SBS Arabic that he understood the government wanted greater control over migration involving international students' families but was concerned about broad restrictions.

"I recognise there is an issue with international students' families' immigration, and I understand that the federal government is trying to control it," he said.

"However, as an international student who used to live with his family, my situation is different."

Alqarni urged the government to examine the data and circumstances of different groups rather than applying broad measures.

"It's a lifetime chance for me to bring my family to Australia and spend a good time with them in Australia," he said.

Rizvi also raised concerns about students undertaking lengthy courses who may be affected by restrictions on bringing partners to Australia.

"If you're doing a four-year nursing degree or a five-year engineering degree or a six-year medicine degree and you're married, to be without your partner for four or six years is really, really difficult," he said.

He argued Australia risked losing some prospective students to competing destinations if they could not bring their partners.

READ MORE Why fixing Australia's immigration system is not just about cutting migrants

Will the changes bring migration down?

The government says the reforms are designed to help bring NOM down to 245,000 this financial year and 225,000 in 2027-28.

Rizvi believes those forecasts will probably be achieved if the changes are combined with the high student visa refusal rates he says have been in place since November 2025.

International students have played a significant role in recent movements in NOM, he said.

"The biggest increase in the big surge in net migration in 2023 was students, and the biggest reduction since then has been students," Rizvi said.

Burke said migration also needed to slow sufficiently for housing supply to "catch up", but rejected the suggestion migration itself was responsible for Australia's housing shortage.

"The housing shortage we have is not caused by immigration," he said.

"But immigration needs to be part of the solution for the housing crisis."

title: 'Absurd': Yoga teachers become an unlikely flashpoint in Australia's migration debate
text:
IN BRIEF The coalition has claimed that Australia was bringing in more yoga teachers than tradies.

Tony Burke addressed the claim at a National Press Club speech, saying it was a "silly" argument.

Amid an ongoing political battle over which party's at fault for a lack of housing and migration numbers, an unlikely target has emerged: yoga teachers.

Labor has been accused by the Opposition of prioritising bringing in instructors of the flexible exercise to Australia, over construction workers sorely needed to address a critical housing shortage.

The Coalition since 2024 has levelled claims against Labor of putting instructors for martial arts and yoga ahead of tradies like bricklayers, painters, roof tilers and stonemasons in the visa queue.

The origins of the political line of attack appeared to come from a Nine Newspaper report which said in 2024 that a federal agency, Jobs and Skills Australia, listed yoga teachers as a skill in demand. Former coalition MP Michael Sukkar highlighted the report on social media, saying: "Under Labor they'll be more Yoga teachers and less tradies!".

On Thursday, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke sought to put the claims to bed, once and for all.

"It is absurd," he told the National Press Club, saying it was among the "silliest of all" arguments.

Burke outlined that rather than deprioritising construction workers, the government had tripled the number it was bringing in, from 4,500 to 15,000.

"In the life of this government, the number of yoga teachers we have brought in is zero," he said.

"Zero. And yet this claim is constantly made about yoga teachers."

According to a fact check from Australian Associated Press (AAP) newswire, the opposition housing spokesman Andrew Bragg and colleagues made the claim a number of times in the past year, saying the government was bringing in more yoga teachers than construction workers.

"While this figure may include yoga teachers, it could also cover coaches of other sports such as basketball or cricket," it said in an August finding.

Yoga teachers came under the temporary skilled visa program in 2022 after the Morrison government signed a trade agreement with India. The places are reserved for Indian nationals under that deal.

"It's a tiny argument, but it is so constantly out there and so demonstrably wrong, it gives an indication as to how a debate like this can just run out of control," Burke said.

title: Cuts, punishment powers and a notable exception: Key changes in Labor's migration shake-up
text:
In brief The federal government has announced a suite of changes to Australia's immigration policy settings.

Working holidaymakers, visa overstayers and students are among those most affected.

The federal government has announced a shake-up of Australia's migration system, with visa-hoppers, overstayers, students, and backpackers targeted in the crackdown.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke unveiled the changes during a National Press Club address on Thursday, following weeks of delay, heated debate and speculation.

Burke began his speech by highlighting the contribution of migration to Australia, but acknowledging there were problems with the current policy settings.

Here's what you need to know:

What's changing?

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Burke said the reforms are split into three parts: who arrives, who stays and who leaves.

Among the most consequential changes are those affecting students, backpackers, visa overstayers and visa hoppers.

International students and those on graduate visas will no longer be able to bring family members with them to Australia, with some exceptions for PhD students and some Pacific and ASEAN students.

The changes are not retrospective and apply only to future students.

"We're not going to be breaking up families on shore," he said.

As part of a so-called "visa-hopping" crackdown, Burke said the government will introduce a qualification scale, meaning only foreign students transferring to higher-level courses (bachelor's to master's for example) will be able to extend their visas.

Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke announced the changes at the National Press Club on Thursday. Source: AAP / Lukas Coch

A ballot system and cap will be introduced for backpackers wishing to extend their visit to a second or third year.

Only 45,000 working holiday-makers will be able to stay in Australia for a second year, and only 5,000 for a third year — down from 57,000 and 31,000 respectively. This will not affect United Kingdom citizens under the rules of a free trade agreement.

The government has already slowed down the processing of working holiday visas, with applications now taking months to be approved. Burke said processing of second-and third-year visas will be restored to the previous, faster pace — with the exception of UK citizens, who are exempt from regional work requirements to secure a visa extension.

The number of UK backpackers has risen sharply since the free trade agreement came into effect in 2023, from about 17,000 in 2021 to just under 80,000 now.

People who overstay their visas, of whom there are about 77,000, will face tougher sanctions, including detention. The government is now looking for more facilities, compliance officers and beds.

Burke said this was a return to a pre-2015 model, when visa overstayers would be taken into detention, and within a few weeks, organise their own flight and leave.

"That didn't just affect them. It had a behavioural impact," he said.

However, he said it would not involve "the sort of operation that some people have seen on TV happening in other countries", an apparent reference to the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations, which have involved mass deportation operations, arrests, and third-country removals.

Powers to punish dodgy migration agents who help with applications they know have no merit will be expanded, including deregistration.

The points test, which determines which skilled migrants are admitted to Australia, will be revamped to treat construction-related qualifications as equivalent to university degrees.

Tweaks to ministerial directions will also prioritise visa applicants with in-demand skills, including in healthcare, construction, education and law enforcement.

Why the changes?

The government is trying to bring Australia's Net Overseas Migration, which represents population growth due to migration, down from 292,100 to 245,000 in the year to July 2027 and 225,000 each year thereafter, and to curb visa-hopping, "rorting" and "gaming" the system.

That figure has stubbornly exceeded Labor's forecasts since the party came to power in 2022, but Burke said migration was now tracking in line with its targets.

The Coalition wants the target to be about 170,000, in line with housing construction, and One Nation wants a 130,000-person-a-year cap.

Burke said immigrants were not to blame for Australia's housing crisis, but said immigration needed to slow down so that housing had a chance to catch up.

How are the changes being implemented?

Some of the changes will come under improved ministerial powers, but others may not become law because negotiations between Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Opposition leader Angus Taylor broke down in the week before Burke's address, dooming hope of getting reforms through the Senate.

Without parliament's approval, the government cannot proceed with restrictions on phoney asylum-seekers' claims.

But Burke insisted negotiations with the Coalition were ongoing and productive, and said: "We have put nothing forward that is a wedge to them."

What has the reaction been?

Kon Karapanagiotidis, CEO and founder of the Asylum Seeker Resource Centre, said the announced changes marked "a dark day for multicultural Australia".

"Today our government chose to turn on migrants, international students and people seeking asylum who have built lives here, contributed to this country and asked for nothing more than the chance to belong," he said in a statement.

The National Farmers' Federation (NFF) said changes to backpacker visas risked Australia's food security, farm safety and regional economies which rely heavily on working holidaymakers.

"This is not how serious policy is made. You do not switch off, slow down or redesign an important workforce pathway on the eve of harvest and expect farmers, contractors, processors and regional communities to absorb the damage," NFF president Hamish McIntyre said.

His comments were echoed by the NFF Horticulture Council executive officer Richard Shannon, who warned of a spike in food prices if the agricultural sector faced a worker shortfall.

"Backpackers doing harvest work in regional Australia are not the cause of housing shortages in our capital cities. They are the reason fruit gets picked, packed and onto supermarket shelves," he said.

Earlier this week, Universities Australia chief Luke Sheehy said political parties competing to cut international student numbers needed to be honest about what Australia would lose.

"A vote for dramatically fewer international students is a vote for a poorer, less skilled Australia," he said.

"You can't take skills, jobs and billions of dollars of economic activity out of the country and pretend there will be no consequences."

— With additional reporting by the Australian Associated Press

title: Ed Sheeran rarely talks politics. The Macklemore controversy has put him at the centre of it
text:
IN BRIEF Sheeran says his concerts aren't a "political forum", but the Macklemore fallout has put that position under scrutiny.

What began with Macklemore saying "Free Palestine" on stage has grown into a wider dispute involving several artists.

Ed Sheeran has built one of the world's biggest music careers while largely avoiding one of the more divisive parts of modern celebrity: politics.

The English singer has spoken publicly about some causes over the years, including performing at a major benefit concert for Ukraine following Russia's 2022 invasion. But he has generally resisted using his concerts as a political platform, something he says is deliberate.

Now, Macklemore's removal from his United States tour has drawn Sheeran into a political debate he has largely sought to avoid.

In less than two weeks, Macklemore has made a high-profile pro-Palestinian speech while opening for Sheeran, been removed from his remaining US tour dates, and been followed out the door by four other acts.

Sheeran has insisted the decision to remove the American rapper wasn't his and says he spent days trying to prevent it.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

But the fallout has nevertheless dragged the 35-year-old singer into a highly charged debate over the Israel-Gaza conflict, antisemitism and the role, or responsibility, of artists to use their platforms to take a political stand.

And it has forced Sheeran to publicly explain why, unlike Macklemore, he generally chooses not to.

"I have my personal views on this devastating conflict," Sheeran wrote in a lengthy statement posted to Instagram this week.

"Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn't mean I don't have them, and it doesn't mean I don't care."

Embroiled in the controversy

The dispute began on 4 September, when Macklemore was performing as a support act on Sheeran's Loop Tour at a New Jersey stadium.

Introducing his 2024 protest song Hind's Hall, the rapper told the crowd that part of the reason he wanted to join the tour was to use its enormous stadium audiences to amplify his support for Palestinians.

"A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: 'Free Palestine'," Macklemore said.

The following day, he again addressed the conflict, telling Jewish members of the audience that his criticism of Israel was not criticism of them.

The remarks sparked a backlash, with the Israeli-American Council launching a petition calling for Macklemore to be removed from the tour, arguing Sheeran's stage should not be used for "one-sided political propaganda".

Macklemore has rejected accusations that his comments were antisemitic.

By Monday, he was off the tour. Promoter Messina Touring Group said venue owners hosting upcoming dates had indicated they would not allow shows featuring Macklemore to proceed.

Sheeran's attempt to stay out of politics

The episode has highlighted the starkly different approaches the two artists take to their public platforms.

Macklemore has become increasingly outspoken about Gaza and has framed speaking about Palestinians from the stage as a moral obligation.

Sheeran, meanwhile, said this week that people attending his concerts "do not expect a political forum".

"I respect Macklemore's strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes," he said.

"However, there is room for multiple approaches to the same end: peace."

READ MORE Israeli minister calls for Oscar-winning film directors to be stripped of citizenship

Sheeran said he instead wants his shows to provide "safety and sanctuary" and bring together people from different backgrounds.

That doesn't mean Sheeran has always avoided political issues or humanitarian causes. In 2022, he performed at the televised Concert for Ukraine, which raised millions for people affected by Russia's invasion. He has also previously spoken publicly on issues including Brexit and LGBTQ+ equality.

But the singer has long resisted being characterised primarily as a political artist.

'I am not complicit'

Sheeran has also rejected suggestions he personally silenced Macklemore.

He said Macklemore had been allowed to choose his own setlist and that his contract for the tour was with the promoter.

Sheeran said he spent the week speaking with venues and was involved in discussions with promoters and activists on both sides in an effort to find a solution that would allow the tour to continue.

Ultimately, he said, the venues and promoter made the final decision.

"Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter's decision, it was not mine," Sheeran said.

"I am not complicit."

Artists walk away from Sheeran's tour

The dispute has now spread beyond Macklemore, with several artists withdrawing from Sheeran's tour in solidarity.

According to Reuters, singer-songwriter Finneas, Danish band Lukas Graham and Irish singer Aaron Rowe have pulled out, while Irish band Beoga — which had been serving as Sheeran's touring band — is also leaving.

"Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed," Finneas said.

Rowe and Beoga both invoked Ireland's history in explaining their decisions.

Sheeran said he had spent the week trying to find a way forward that would allow Macklemore (pictured) to remain on the tour, including speaking directly with venues, promoters and activists on both sides of the issue. Credit: Invision

Beoga said its members were "Irish people who understand colonialism" and pointed to their involvement with the Irish Artists for Palestine movement.

Rowe, who described Sheeran as a friend who had changed his life, said he could not stand by while powerful people silenced those who spoke out.

Lukas Graham described its withdrawal as a "difficult decision", while arguing that wealth should not determine who was able to participate in public debate.

Why was Macklemore removed?

Macklemore has long publicly supported Palestinians and criticised Israel's military campaign in Gaza and its occupation of the West Bank.

In 2024, he released the protest song Hind's Hall in solidarity with pro-Palestinian demonstrators and in memory of five-year-old Palestinian girl Hind Rajab, who was killed in Gaza.

Macklemore has claimed New England Patriots NFL team owner Robert Kraft, whose Massachusetts stadium is hosting two upcoming Sheeran concerts, rallied stadium owners against his involvement in the tour.

READ MORE Australia sanctions Israeli extremists in response to violence in Palestine

Kraft has said he has dedicated significant time to fighting hate and antisemitism and felt a responsibility to intervene when he believed "that line has been crossed". Reuters reported Kraft had not publicly addressed Macklemore's specific claim that he rallied other stadium owners.

Pro-Israeli groups and US singer Pink, who is Jewish, have also criticised Macklemore, arguing comments made at concerts could compromise the safety of Jewish and pro-Israeli attendees.

Critics have also pointed to a 2014 appearance in which Macklemore wore a costume featuring a black wig, beard and fake hooked nose, which was criticised for invoking antisemitic stereotypes. Macklemore later apologised.

Macklemore has denied his recent comments were antisemitic, arguing that criticism of Israel's actions should not be conflated with antisemitism.

Sheeran's US tour is scheduled to resume in Philadelphia on 19 September.

title: From 'cashies' to convictions: The ATO's $2.7 million warning shot
text:
Key Points More than 350 individuals or businesses have been successfully prosecuted as part of a shadow economy crackdown.

The prosecutions related to tax avoidance and underpayment of entitlements.

Hundreds of people and businesses have been prosecuted for tax offences, with millions of dollars in fines handed down as authorities crack down on the shadow economy.

The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) on Thursday revealed non-lodgment prosecutions against "dodgy shadow economy operators" had risen by 80 per cent over the past two years, as it warned those who broke the rules would be held accountable.

The shadow economy involves both legal and illegal economic activity, including demanding cash payments for work, known as "cashies", to avoid tax, and underpayment of entitlements such as superannuation.

The ATO said more than 350 individuals or businesses had been successfully prosecuted in the past two years, resulting in more than $2.7 million in fines.

In the 2025-26 financial year, Queensland accounted for 28 per cent of non-lodgment prosecutions, followed by Western Australia (26 per cent) and NSW (20 per cent).

"The shadow economy undermines legitimate businesses and reduces revenue that would otherwise fund essential public services that support all Australians," he said.

"It doesn't matter what profession you're in, if you're a tradie, hairdresser or cafe owner, and you deliberately avoid paying the right amount of tax, you risk more than financial penalties."

Of the prosecutions, more than 305 resulted in convictions, representing a nearly 60 per cent increase from 2024–25 and 2025–26 financial years.

Goding said the figures demonstrated the ATO was holding those who break the rules to account.

"We've seen business owners receive criminal convictions, lose the trust of their customers and community, and in some cases, lose the very business they were trying to keep afloat. For more serious offending, time in prison is even a possibility.

"Our message to the community is clear: deliberately ignoring your obligations comes at a significant cost."

A 2016 government task force estimated Australia's shadow economy could be worth as much as 3 per cent of GDP, or approximately $50 billion in 2016 figures.

More recent ATO estimates show the shadow economy has continued to grow, reaching up to 5.4 per cent of GDP in 2023.

title: Tony Burke unveils major migration changes to tighten Australia's visa system — as it happened
text:
Changes to points system, backpacker visa processing

Burke said the reforms are split into three parts: who arrives, who stays and who leaves.

Changes will be made to the points test, a scoring system used to rank and select skilled workers for visas, with those with housing trade qualifications receiving the same number of points as a university qualification.

Construction, agriculture, fisheries, resources, and teaching will also be prioritised.

"The fact we are doing that allows us to restore the normal processing speed that we were previously at for primary applications for working holiday-makers," he said.

Working holiday maker visa approvals have slowed, and Burke said faster processing will be restored for those in their second or third year who are required to work regionally.

He said that the remote work requirement does not apply to working holiday-makers from the United Kingdom under a free trade agreement, noting the number of UK backpackers has exploded.

"Just to give you a sense of the pace of the growth, at the time that the free trade agreement was signed, the number of UK backpackers we had here in Australia was in the order of 17,000," he said.

"Now that's a little bit on the low side, so that was the end of the pandemic. But the previous peak had been around 35,000. It's now just shy of 80,000 in terms of numbers of people here in Australia.

"It's a level of growth that means we are just at the moment going to continue to be processing that one slowly."

He said the federal government was having conversations with UK counterparts about it in a "constructive way".

title: US Federal Reserve raises interest rates for the first time since 2023, defying Trump
text:
In brief Experts anticipate at least one more rate hike by the US Federal Reserve by the end of this year.

The decision is likely to ease doubts that the Fed chief would hold off on tighter policy out of deference to Trump.

United States President Donald Trump has demanded interest rates be cut to 1 per cent after the US Federal Reserve raised interest rates on Thursday for the first time since 2023.

The Fed voted unanimously to raise rates by 0.25 percentage points, saying the rate hike would support a "timelier return" to its 2 per cent target for inflation.

It was a blow for Trump, who appointed central bank chief Kevin Warsh in the hopes that he would lower rates.

Instead, in his first major decision, the opposite was done.

Trump took to his social media platform Truth Social to speak out against the rise, saying rates should be less than 1 per cent and that the US could no longer "carry" other countries.

But he stopped short of criticising Warsh personally.

"Interest Rates in the United States should be 1%, or less, because we are the Best Credit in the World — BY FAR," Trump wrote on Thursday morning.

United States Donald Trump took to social media to say interest rates needed to be lowered — "and fast". Source: Truth Social / Donald Trump

He said that if they stopped trading with countries with a deficit, the US would make "at least" US$1.5 trillion ($2.1 trillion) a year. He did not cite a source for that figure.

"We are "carrying" almost every country in the World, and that cannot go on any longer," he added, before ending with: "LOWER THE INTEREST RATES FOR THE UNITED STATES OF AMERICA, AND FAST!"

Trump-appointed Warsh defies pressure

It's ‌the first policy shift ‌under the new Fed chief, ⁠who took office in late May after being selected by Trump with an expectation that he would cut rates.

Warsh stressed the need to combat inflation that has been "too high" for "too long" and said the decision was a "serious" one, but needed to be taken.

"The plain fact is that inflation is too high, and has been for too long," he told a press conference.

And the hike may not be the last — the vast majority of Fed policymakers indicated that at least one more rate hike was likely necessary before the end of the year, according to their Summary of Economic Projections.

US households and businesses have been battered by years of higher-than-target inflation, and prices have surged in the wake of Trump's war on Iran, his signature tariff policies and the ongoing AI boom.

Trump has launched an unprecedented assault on the Fed's independence since taking office, attempting to fire a Fed governor and launching a criminal probe against Warsh's predecessor in his quest for lower rates to spur economic activity.

Trump's Republican Party faces a stern test in the upcoming midterm elections, with rival Democrats seeking to wrest control of both houses of Congress and with economic issues front and centre for voters.

White House calls rate hike decision 'unfortunate'

US stock markets largely priced in Thursday's rate hike, but they were still down on the news — expected with any rate hike as equities become less attractive.

Yields on 10-year US Treasury bonds — which have surged in recent days as uncertainty on long-term inflation has spiked — were also up past the 5 per cent threshold.

Following the Fed's announcement, White House spokesperson Kush Desai said the decision was "rather unfortunate" and that Trump had been clear that he wanted lower interest rates.

Warsh was named to his position after a contentious Senate confirmation process, where Democratic lawmakers accused him of being a "sock puppet" for Trump, which he denied.

So far, Trump has supported Warsh, claiming that the Fed chair wants lower rates and accusing the board of being "political."

The Fed has a dual mandate to deliver maximum employment while keeping inflation to its long-term 2 per cent target.

It mainly achieves these goals by setting the key US interest rate — lower rates tend to spur economic activity but fuel inflation, and hiking them cools both activity and prices.

title: 'Mobilisation of fear': The deeper strategy behind One Nation's immigration policy
text:
This audio is voiced by AI and may occasionally mispronounce words.

Jyoti has called her migration agent three times this month. Each time, she asks the same question: Has there been any update?

Her application for a Skilled Independent visa, a pathway to permanent residency, has been sitting in the queue for months. It has felt like a long wait for Jyoti, who has lived in Australia for the better part of a decade. In recent months, that uncertainty has taken on a new urgency.

The 43-year-old is a secondary school teacher who lives in an outer northern suburb of Melbourne with her husband and their two children. She arrived from Punjab, northern India, eight years ago as an international student and is now in Australia on a work visa.

She asks that only her first name be used because she fears speaking publicly could affect her family's visa prospects.

I feel like the axe is going to fall on people like us before anyone else.

"International students, temporary visa holders ... we would be the first to lose our livelihoods and our place here if Pauline Hanson comes to power, or if her party keeps gaining momentum," she tells SBS News.

Jyoti says she is watching the lead-up to Victoria's November election closely. To her, the election will be an early test of how far One Nation leader Pauline Hanson's momentum could travel and what that could mean for her family's future in the only country her children have really known. It's a fear, she says, that everyone she knows in her position is carrying right now.

READ MORE Why fixing Australia's immigration system is not just about cutting migrants

One Nation wants to cut 750,000 temporary visa holders from Australia over three years. Not one of them will get a say in whether the party succeeds.

"Our fate is being decided by political parties whose fate we have no say in," Jyoti says.

Australia is home to roughly three million temporary visa holders, including students, graduates and skilled workers.

As One Nation pushes for sweeping cuts to temporary migration, it raises a harder question about political power: are people with the least ability to influence an election also the easiest to target?

Who One Nation's visa cuts would hit hardest

One Nation's plan would tighten the student and graduate visa systems, restrict family members from accompanying temporary skilled workers, and close off "visa hopping" — the practice of extending a stay by switching between visa categories rather than leaving the country and reapplying offshore.

According to the policy announced on Monday, international students and graduates would absorb the biggest cuts.

The student visa population, including accompanying family members, would fall from about 590,000 to 350,000, and the graduate visa population from about 270,000 to just 40,000 over three years.

Family visas linked to temporary skilled workers would be phased out entirely, a change expected to shrink that cohort from about 263,000 to 160,000 over the same period.

Source: SBS News

"Tinkering around the edges will not fix the damage," Hanson said in the media release.

"This is about giving Australians breathing space by drastically cutting the stock of temporary migrants, restoring control and making sure migration serves Australia."

Speaking with ABC's Radio National on Monday morning, Environment Minister Murray Watt said One Nation's policy would trigger economic disruption.

"One Nation's policy is a recipe to destroy the Australian economy and drive the Australian economy into recession," he said.

For people already living that reality, the question isn't abstract. Jyoti says the proposed changes have made getting permanent residency feel less like the obvious next step in her journey and more like a race against time.

They are looking at us as just numbers, but there are actual lives and people behind these numbers.

Not everyone would be affected equally, says Abul Rizvi, a former deputy secretary of the Department of Immigration. Much depends on a migrant's professional skills and experience.

"Temporary entrants with skills in strong demand tend to secure permanent residency much faster than others," he tells SBS News.

Abul Rizvi, a former deputy secretary of the Department of Immigration, says One Nation's immigration policy would significantly affect Australia's education industry, which relies heavily on international students. Source: SBS News / Ewa Staszewska

For instance, a nurse's pathway to permanent residency looks nothing like that of a graduate in a field with weaker demand. For the latter, the road can be far longer, and far less certain.

One Nation has confirmed it would maintain a net overseas migration (NOM) ceiling of 130,000 a year once its proposed three-year reset is complete.

Rizvi says that target leaves the policy with nowhere else to land.

"Taking into account the fact that One Nation has said it wants to quarantine WHMs [Working Holiday Makers] and PALM [Pacific Australia Labour Mobility] visas from any cuts; cannot lawfully reduce places for partners and dependent children; can't easily reduce numbers of NZ citizens contributing to NOM and wants to maintain a flow of tradies and health workers, it leaves no room for students and temporary graduates," he says.

Essentially, One Nation policy would mean abolishing the international education industry.

"That would have massive consequences for university budgets and staff. Possibly 50,000 jobs would be directly affected. More indirectly."

The political cost of having no vote

Temporary entrants have never had voting rights in Australia and "never will", Rizvi says.

But it's a dynamic that has shaped migration policy for longer than many realise, says Emily Foley, a postdoctoral research fellow at the University of Canberra who studies social democratic and centre-left political parties.

She says temporary migration has quietly created problems over many decades that successive governments have had little reason to confront.

Emily Foley says temporary migration quietly created problems that governments had "minimal political incentive" to address. Source: Supplied

"For years, policymakers and governments knew there were significant issues with the temporary migration program essentially creating an underclass of exploited and marginalised workers," she tells SBS News.

"And yet, precisely because this cohort are not voters, there was minimal political incentive to actively discuss the policy area, particularly when migration was such a salient and politicised election issue."

One Nation is not alone in pushing for tighter controls on temporary migration. Labor has already moved to amend parts of its policy, including restricting visa hopping, shortening Temporary Graduate visas, raising the income threshold for temporary skilled migration and introducing managed limits on new international student commencements.

The Coalition has also promised to reduce migration by linking NOM to the number of homes built. It has separately proposed making compliance with an Australian Values Statement a universal visa condition, with breaches potentially leading to visa refusal or cancellation.

But One Nation's proposal goes considerably further, targeting the temporary migrant population with sharp reductions in student and graduate numbers and restrictions on accompanying family members.

Foley says the party's focus is consistent with its longstanding position on immigration.

Attacking temporary migrants is therefore not surprising.

"This cohort, despite many being Australian taxpayers, are without the civil, political and economic rights and privileges of Australian citizens and permanent residents. It is easy for parties like One Nation to attack and marginalise temporary migrants precisely because they have so little recourse."

Benjamin Moffitt, a senior lecturer in politics and international relations at Monash University, is more blunt about the electoral calculus.

"It removes the one thing that usually keeps rhetoric in check: the people it hits getting a vote on it," he tells SBS News.

"Temporary visa holders and prospective migrants can't punish a party at the ballot box, so there's no electoral cost to going as hard as you like on them.

"That's true of migration policy generally, not a One Nation quirk, but it's a big part of why this is the one area where the inflammatory rhetoric can run so far ahead of the actual policy detail."

Benjamin Moffitt says political parties understand that temporary visa holders and prospective migrants have no direct electoral leverage because they cannot vote. Source: Supplied / Nish Paranavitana

But he stops short of saying One Nation is deliberately targeting temporary migrants for this reason.

What can be established, Moffitt says, is that the groups One Nation has identified most precisely — including international students, working holidaymakers and skilled visa holders — are among those who cannot vote.

"Whether that's a deliberate strategy of picking targets who can't retaliate, or simply where the populist radical right's usual scapegoating logic lands by default, isn't something you can necessarily tell apart from the outside."

One Nation did not respond to SBS News' request for comment on whether the lack of voting rights among temporary visa holders is a consideration in its immigration policies.

What temporary migrants contribute

Temporary migrants make up a significant part of Australia's workforce and international education sector. Their contribution extends beyond the visa system , with international students alone generating almost $55 billion in education export income in 2025.

According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, international students and their families accounted for 82.4 per cent of non-residents eligible to work in Australia in June 2025.

Andrew McKellar, CEO of the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry, told reporters on Monday that cutting temporary migration to the degree proposed by One Nation could have a significant economic impact.

"You know, if you're going to cut overall visa levels by 750,000 over a three-year period and drive net overseas migration into negative territory, that's a COVID-level shock to the Australian economy," he said.

One Nation has pointed to Canada's recent cuts to temporary migration as evidence that immigration can be reduced without crashing the economy.

McKellar said the focus should instead be on the potential impact of the proposed cuts on Australia's growth.

"What the debate cannot be about is it cannot be about arbitrary targets. We can't have solutions which are extreme, which would cause very significant damage to the Australian economy."

Why immigration works for One Nation

Tiziana Torresi is the program director of the School of Society and Culture at Adelaide University and studies normative political theory and the governance of migration. She says immigration sits within a broader populist strategy that divides society between an "authentic" Australian public and groups portrayed as threatening to its interests.

"Anti-immigration rhetoric has been central to One Nation's political discourse from its emergence," she tells SBS News.

Tiziana Torresi says the One Nation's appeal taps into Australian voters' economic and social anxieties. Source: Supplied

Torresi says the party's appeal taps into economic and social anxieties.

"The mobilisation of fear is a key strategy of populist far-right parties, enabling them to present themselves as the only true voice and defenders of an authentic national community threatened by 'outsiders'," she says.

Moffitt says this extends to issues such as housing, jobs and infrastructure. He describes this approach as 'nativism', where social and economic problems are attributed to outsiders, particularly migrants.

"Nativism doesn't identify a housing crisis and then, separately, decide migrants are to blame; it needs a scapegoat for social and economic ills, and the migrant is the figure built to supply one," he says.

The result is a message that can speak to voters worried about the cost of living, housing and population growth, while also tapping into deeper concerns about Australia's changing social and cultural identity.

Torresi says this allows One Nation to present itself as the party willing to restore a sense of control to voters who believe established political parties have failed them.

One Nation can exploit these various anxieties by claiming that 'ordinary Australians' are being left behind or displaced.

That is where the politics of temporary migration becomes more complicated. The people most directly affected may have no vote, but the issue is being used to speak to millions of people who do.

Beyond the ballot box

Torresi says the absence of a vote does not mean migrants are politically disconnected.

"Migrants are embedded in families, workplaces, neighbourhoods, unions, community organisations, and broader social networks, creating relationships with citizens who do possess electoral rights," she says.

Those relationships can give migrants an indirect political voice through the citizens around them, who can respond at the ballot box.

"Consequently, political attacks on migrants may have effects that extend well beyond the migrant population itself."

But temporary migrants may have fewer connections to Australian citizens who can advocate for their interests, Torresi says.

"Temporary migrants may be doubly vulnerable to anti-immigration politics because they can lack both direct and indirect forms of political influence."

Back in Melbourne, Jyoti says the fear she feels is being mirrored back to her.

"It's not just me. Everyone I know in this situation feels the same fear," she says.

We've built our lives here, and none of that means we get a say in what happens to us next.

Her migration agent still doesn't have an update. She'll call again next week.

title: An ancient disease is surging in Australia — and it isn't always easy to detect
text:
IN BRIEF Gonorrhoea and syphilis notifications have surged by more than half in the past decade.

Indigenous health experts have warned of a serious need for investment in community-led health projects.

Reported cases of infectious syphilis and gonorrhoea have surged by more than half over the past decade in Australia, as experts warn education and testing urgently needs to improve.

In 2025, there were 42,393 gonorrhoea notifications and 5,986 infectious syphilis notifications — a 10-year increase of 57 per cent for gonorrhoea and 56 per cent for syphilis, analysis from the University of New South Wales' Kirby Institute has shown.

Syphilis was declared a communicable disease of national significance in late 2025, in response to "ongoing and concerning" rises in Australian case numbers.

Chief medical officer Professor Michael Kidd declared that awareness was necessary among all Australians, including healthcare professionals, and urged everyone to get tested.

Syphilis and gonorrhoea are common bacterial infections with ancient origins, now easily treated with antibiotics.

But both infections can present with either mild or non-existent symptoms.

If left untreated, syphilis progresses through stages and can spread to the brain, heart, eyes, and other organs. It can cause neurological problems including paralysis, and dementia, and cause soft, tumour-like growths to appear on the skin, bones or internal organs. Tertiary syphilis can eventually lead to death.

Chlamydia remained the most frequently diagnosed STI in 2025, followed by gonorrhoea, then syphilis. Source: SBS News / The Kirby Institute

Notification rates for infectious syphilis among women increased 170 per cent in the past decade from 2016 to 2025. In contrast, rates increased just 39 per cent among males.

Syphilis during pregnancy can lead to congenital syphilis, which can result in miscarriage or stillbirth, or severe lifelong health impacts in babies that are born, including prematurity, low birthweight and other physical developmental abnormalities.

Kirby Institute epidemiologist Dr Skye McGregor said congenital syphilis is a persistent issue in Australia, with more than half of deaths in the last decade among First Nations infants. There were 14 cases of congenital syphilis in 2025, and 113 from 2016 to 2025, with 40 resulting in the death of an infant.

"This is an entirely preventable outcome with early diagnosis, testing and treatment of pregnant people," McGregor said.

Better approaches for at-risk populations

First Nations peoples were disproportionately affected by STIs, diagnosed with gonorrhoea at more than four times the rate of non-Indigenous people and syphilis at more than six times.

Kim Gates, community relations lead in the Kirby Institute's First Nations Point-Of-Care Program, said the disparities in diagnoses between First Nations and non-Indigenous Australians were an indication of broader inequities in healthcare.

READ MORE Stolen Generations survivors face worse health outcomes than other First Nations people

Australian services needed to be designed better to reflect the experiences of First Nations communities, Gates told SBS News, adding that many First Nations peoples have a complex relationship with the Australian health system and "have good reasons to be sceptical of top-down services and approaches".

"This is why Aboriginal-led services are so important," she said.

Gates said that while the 149 Aboriginal Controlled Community Health Services in Australia provide comprehensive and culturally safe healthcare, "there are areas these don't reach".

READ MORE This Australian crisis is entering a 'confronting' new phase

For Gates, sustained investment in community-led initiatives, like the First Nations Molecular Point-of-Care Testing Program, was the solution to bringing down STI rates among Indigenous populations.

Improving community awareness is key

Dr Arthur Wong, sexual health physician and conjoint lecturer at the Kirby Institute, said that timely testing, treatment and retesting were "crucial", and that post-diagnosis care was also "essential" to avoid repeat infections.

Wong told SBS News that awareness was already affecting syphilis rates, where evidence shows a decline in incidence among gay and bisexual men.

"We do know that testing has increased in certain populations," Wong said. "Gay and bisexual men who are taking HIV pre-exposure prophylaxis (PReP) are tested more frequently for STIs."

But the data leaves out an often-overlooked section of the population — for homosexual, bisexual and transgender women, rates of syphilis and gonorrhoea remain largely unknown.

LGBTIQ+ Women's Project Lead at ACON (formerly AIDS Council of NSW), Lee Wang, says queer and trans women aren't routinely reported in surveillance data, which has adverse health outcomes.

"When queer and trans women are overlooked, it can create the false impression that STI prevention and testing are not relevant to them," Wang told SBS News.

"This can contribute to lower testing and missed opportunities for prevention and early diagnosis, with recent surveys highlighting substantial gaps in STI testing when compared with gay and bisexual men."

There was a need for targeted sexual health education resources, Wang said, like ACON's Word on the Sheets, a digital sexual and reproductive health resource for LGBTQ+ women, trans and gender diverse people.

"We shouldn't confuse a lack of data with a lack of priority," Wang said. "We need healthcare providers who are equipped to discuss sexual practices without making assumptions about sexuality or gender identity."

Wong said preliminary data from the most recent Australian Study of Health and Relationships show that just 17 per cent of people aged 16 to 49 reported having an STI test in the last 12 months.

Rates of chlamydia and gonorrhoea were highest among young people aged 15 to 29 years.

Studies in recent years have pointed to a waning use of condoms among school-aged people in Australia, with findings from a Secondary Students and Sexual Health (SSASH) survey analysis by Victoria University in 2024 stating that condom use in Australia was low and has declined over a decade.

Overall, Wong said, Australia needed a "sustained and enhanced" response to sexual health, "to ensure any gains are experienced equally across all populations."

title: EU proposes landmark associate membership for Canada
text:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the European Union is opening the door for Canada to become its first "associate member", a status that is not set out in the bloc's treaties.

Von der Leyen's announcement is a significant shift in EU policy. The bloc has historically resisted flexible categories and EU members were lukewarm in reacting to Germany's proposal in May of associate membership for Ukraine as a stepping stone to full accession.

"Partnerships are a strategic choice for Europe. But they also respond to the fracture in the international rules-based system," von der Leyen said in her annual State of the European Union address to the European Parliament in Strasbourg.

"We see the world with the same eyes: from AI to climate change, from the Arctic to geopolitics. And we have stood together: on Ukraine, on defence, on raw materials and on supply chains. But above all ... Europe and Canada believe in democracy."

Canada's Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier this week Canada was seeking a "unique alliance" with the EU but not membership. Von der Leyen invited Carney to join her in Strasbourg, and he will make his own address on Thursday.

title: 'Really problematic': Australians are rejecting the very homes the country needs
text:
IN BRIEF New home sales fell 10 per cent in August and are now at their lowest level in more than a year.

Experts say high borrowing and construction costs are making the new homes Australia needs harder to afford.

Buyers appear to be rejecting newly-built homes, sparking concerns Australia's property market slowdown could worsen a chronic housing shortage.

Sales of new homes fell 10 per cent nationally in August and were 19.3 per cent lower in the three months to August compared with the previous quarter, according to new data from the Housing Industry Association (HIA).

Sales have now fallen for four consecutive months to their lowest level in more than a year.

The slowdown was recorded across all five mainland states included in the HIA survey, which tracks sales by large-volume home builders and is considered a leading indicator of future detached home construction.

Victoria recorded the sharpest quarterly decline, with sales down 27 per cent, followed by Queensland at 20.2 per cent, NSW at 17.5 per cent, South Australia at 10.8 per cent and Western Australia at 8.2 per cent.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

HIA chief economist Tim Reardon said the deterioration meant the recovery in new home building seen earlier this year had been interrupted.

"Today's new home sales are tomorrow's housing commencements," he said in a statement.

"The decline in sales through the middle of 2026 will mean fewer homes commencing construction in 2027."

Why are Australians pulling back?

Independent property economist Cameron Kusher told SBS News that a combination of higher borrowing costs and low confidence was making it increasingly difficult to buy a new home. But he warned that if sales continued to decline leading to fewer builds, it could lead to even higher prices in the future.

"We're seeing really weak confidence around the housing market generally at the moment," he told SBS News.

Tim Lawless, the research director at property data firm Cotality, said the slowdown was also evident across the broader property market, although new homes appeared to have been hit harder.

Cotality estimates home sales across the broader market were about 15 per cent lower over winter than a year earlier and 11 per cent below the five-year average.

"It does look like new home sales have been hit a little bit harder," Lawless said, pointing to higher interest rates, weaker confidence, reduced investment and affordability and serviceability constraints.

The slowdown has been particularly pronounced in Sydney, Brisbane and Perth, where Cotality estimates home sales fell by more than 20 per cent over winter compared with the same period last year.

Lawless said Brisbane and Perth were coming off relatively strong levels of activity, while Sydney's decline was more reflective of severe affordability constraints.

Kusher said new homes typically carried a premium compared with established properties, making older homes more desirable as household borrowing capacity comes under pressure.

"Buyers are asking themselves: "Am I prepared to pay the premium for a brand-new home when I can get an older home, an established home, cheaper?"

"I'm not surprised that we're seeing these ongoing falls, but obviously that's really problematic when you need to be building more homes."

The HIA data does not provide a detailed breakdown of the types or price points of detached homes experiencing the greatest decline.

But Kusher said affordability was clearly becoming a bigger constraint.

Higher interest rates mean some prospective buyers simply aren't able to borrow enough to buy the homes they otherwise might have considered.

HIA has also pointed to rising construction costs, taxation and broader economic uncertainty as factors weighing on the sector.

Reardon said builders were reporting fewer people visiting display sites, declining enquiries and preliminary commitments, and rising cancellation rates.

Lawless agreed, telling SBS News that higher material, labour and other construction costs were also making new homes less competitive with established properties.

Why today's sales matter for tomorrow's housing supply

Government figures show there were 244,000 dwellings under construction in the March quarter of 2026, the most since records began in 1984.

The deterioration in sales is unlikely to immediately show up in housing commencements this year.

The problem comes further down the pipeline, with the impact of weaker sales expected to become more apparent in 2027.

Lawless said some projects may have become financially unviable as construction and labour costs increased, while others may not have secured enough pre-sales to trigger financing.

"Typically most developers would need to have a minimum level of pre-sales before a lender is going to be becoming active in the credit supply," he said.

Kusher said most builders sought to secure a buyer before starting construction rather than building homes speculatively and hoping to sell them afterwards.

Financing speculative construction was particularly difficult when both borrowing and construction costs were high, he said.

That means the relationship between weaker sales and fewer future homes is relatively straightforward.

"If people aren't buying homes, you're not likely to get many homes built," Kusher said.

In 2024 the National Housing Accord commenced with an aspirational target of 1.2 million new, well-located homes over the five years to June 2029.

The target was agreed between federal, state and territory governments, local government and industry in an effort to substantially increase housing supply.

Government figures show this is already behind targets and likely won't be met until the end of 2030, and Kusher warns it could get blown out further still.

Australia needs homes — but at what price?

The slowdown creates a difficult contradiction for Australia's housing market.

Demand has not disappeared simply because fewer people can afford to buy a newly built home.

"The thing with the shortage of supply in housing is that price matters," Kusher said.

"We need more houses, but they need to be at a price that people can afford."

Lawless described the construction sector as being caught "between a rock and a hard place".

"A builder or a developer, obviously, they're not going to be building homes if there's no profit to be had, and consumers or households aren't going to be buying new homes if they're too expensive to purchase," he said.

HIA similarly warned the decline in new home sales was occurring without an equivalent decline in Australia's underlying need for housing, pointing to population growth, low unemployment and the existing shortage of homes.

What could turn the market around?

HIA has warned that further interest rate rises would place additional pressure on a new home market already struggling with weaker demand.

"This is not the time for another rate rise," Reardon said.

Kusher, however, said getting inflation under control was ultimately necessary to restore stability to the housing market — even if doing so meant households faced more financial pressure in the short term.

He said longer-term improvement depended on bringing inflation under control, allowing greater certainty to return to the economy and eventually creating scope for borrowing costs to fall.

"Now that means higher interest rates, and that means it's going to be hard for people."

But he said easing inflation could ultimately provide the conditions needed for both property prices and borrowing costs to stabilise, "and that's when you'll start to see things improve."

title: Nyadol Nyuon responds to criticism over 'no white culture' remarks
text:
IN BRIEF The lawyer says race and culture should not be conflated, arguing there is no single "white culture".

Nyuon previously began returning her OAM as part of what she called her "slow and certain" departure from Australia.

Lawyer and human rights advocate Nyadol Nyuon has defended her claim that there is "no white culture" after remarks she made turning a televised debate drew criticism.

Nyuon appeared on the ABC's National Forum on migration on Monday, where she rejected the idea Australia was historically monocultural and said she had "no intention of assimilating".

But she stressed that did not mean rejecting Australia, its laws or the country she says she "deeply" loves.

She argued that describing Australia as an "Anglo-Celtic culture" risked creating the impression there was a single "white culture" migrants were expected to adopt.

"There is Italian culture, there is French culture, there is Argentinian culture, but there is not this notion of sort of a white culture that is being threatened," Nyuon told the forum.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The discussion came amid a broader national debate about migration, multiculturalism and what it means to be Australian.

Following criticism of her remarks, Nyuon expanded on the argument in a social media post on her LinkedIn account.

'No white culture'

"Apparently, saying there is no white culture has offended some people," she wrote on Tuesday.

"There is no white culture as there is no black culture."

Nyuon argued that race and culture should not be treated as interchangeable, pointing to the cultural differences that exist between people who may otherwise be grouped together according to skin colour.

"Black is a colour, not a culture. There are Black people. There is Ethiopian culture," she wrote.

Nyuon also defended her argument that Australia had never been monocultural, pointing to the hundreds of First Nations that existed before colonisation as well as the long histories of Chinese migrants and Afghan cameleers in Australia.

A debate over belonging

During the forum, former deputy prime minister John Anderson argued there were legitimate concerns among Australians about social cohesion and whether some groups respected Australian culture and values.

Anderson described those values as including individual dignity, equality before the law and the separation of the secular and sacred.

Nyuon acknowledged Australians had a right to be concerned about threats to social cohesion but challenged the way the issue was being framed.

She argued the migration debate could become a proxy for conversations about race and questioned why a person's appearance should influence perceptions of their belonging.

"Whenever we attempt to speak about how our belonging can look like, you meet such resistance, and the majority of the time that resistance comes from how you look," she said on Monday.

'I love this country'

Nyuon also spoke about her complicated relationship with Australia and her previously announced intention to begin the process of renouncing her Australian citizenship.

The lawyer, who was born in a refugee camp in Ethiopia after her family fled the Sudanese civil war, came to Australia as a teenager.

In April, Nyuon revealed she had written to the governor-general's office to begin returning the Medal of the Order of Australia she was awarded in 2022 for "service to human rights and refugee women".

"This is the first step in my slow and certain process of leaving Australia and releasing my connections to this country," she wrote at the time.

Nyuon said she remained "so grateful" to Australia and would "always be indebted to it", but linked her decision to her experiences with Victoria University and WorkSafe Victoria.

Nyuon resigned from Victoria University in 2025, after overseeing an $800,000 WorkSafe Victoria project aimed at preventing workplace gendered violence, which was plagued by delays, strained relationships and resourcing issues.

An independent evaluator later found instability and mismanagement meant it could not properly assess the program's success.

Speaking on National Forum, she said she loved Australia but was conscious that political circumstances could affect whether she and her children felt they could remain.

"Many migrants deeply, deeply love this country. I love this country," she said.

In her subsequent LinkedIn post, Nyuon maintained her comments about culture were not intended as an insult.

title: Minister dodges migration modelling question eight times amid farmers’ fury
text:
Advertisement

Employment Minister Amanda Rishworth has repeatedly failed to say whether Labor modelled the impacts of its new migration plan on wages or the broader economy, despite the government claiming plans proposed by One Nation and the Coalition would damage the Australian economy. Speaking on radio on Friday morning, Rishworth was asked eight times whether the government had modelled the impact on wages of significant cuts to backpacker visas, and the broader economic impact of Labor’s plan, and eight times did not give a direct answer. Employment and Industrial Relations Minister Amanda Rishworth. Dominic Lorrimer In response to repeated questions, Rishworth said she was “not really able to comment” on the modelling, later saying it was a matter for Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke. As minister for both employment and workplace relations, Rishworth has oversight over workers’ wages and is a member of cabinet. Labor has vowed to cut nearly 40,000 backpacker visas per year and crack down on overstayers through increased enforcement as part of a plan that Burke unveiled on Thursday. The Coalition and the National Farmers’ Federation have slammed the overhaul, arguing it will raise the price of food and hurt primary producers.

Advertisement

The new regulations do not lower Labor’s current net overseas migration target, but instead aim to help the government achieve its plan of 245,000 migrants by June next year and then 225,000 by mid-2028. One Nation wants negative migration, followed by an annual net migration figure of 130,000, while the Coalition wants a figure slightly lower than 170,000. One Nation’s plan has been widely condemned as economically reckless. Related Article Immigration What are Labor’s new migration rules for Australia? Net overseas migration is the total number of people entering the country minus the number of people leaving. During her ABC Radio National appearance, Rishworth said the policy amounted to “important and sensible changes” that contributed to a “sustainable” migration policy. Rishworth was unable to say whether there would be a positive impact to domestic workers’ wages or increased wage bills for farmers. Asked a third time about the modelling of wages, Rishworth said: “We always want to see decent wages for workers, but there is a safety net in this country, and if the suggestion is suggesting somehow that backpackers are getting paid under that safety net, then I would find that unacceptable.”

Advertisement

Opposition employment spokeswoman Jane Hume told this masthead that Labor wasn’t serious about lowering migration, and Rishworth had proven it. “Amanda Rishworth is the employment minister, yet she can’t answer a basic question about the impact of her government’s own policy on Australian wages,” Hume said. “If she hasn’t seen the modelling, she should. If it doesn’t exist, Labor should say so. Because otherwise just like inflation and housing, this is just another target Labor will fail to meet.” Zac Herman, a full-time worker on a pistachio farm in Kyalite in the Riverina district of NSW, which relies on migrant workers year round and employs dozens on migrant visas for the harvest. Erin Jonasson Earlier this week, Labor rubbished One Nation’s migration proposal, arguing it could push the Australian economy into recession.

Advertisement

Under Labor’s plan, working holidaymakers or backpackers will face a ballot system to access second- and third-year visa renewals. Second-year places will drop from 57,000 to 45,000, and third-year places will drop from 31,000 to 5000. Kyalite Pistachios general manager Ben Seton-Stewart said his orchard operation was highly dependent on access to a reliable seasonal workforce. He said pruning, crop management, harvesting and processing must be completed within narrow windows and seasonal workers provided essential labour capacity on his farm near Swan Hill, on the Victoria-NSW border. His business has recently moved away from relying primarily on backpackers in favour of labour-hire arrangements. But he said seasonal workers spent money in local communities, making an important economic contribution. “The value of these workers therefore extends well beyond their immediate role in the orchard,” he said.

title: Why I hate ‘top 100’ book lists (and can’t stop reading them)
text:
What is it about these Top 100 book lists? They are absurd. If critics choose them, they reflect only the critics’ tastes. If chosen by the public, they reflect only what people interested in voting have read and liked. You can’t say these are the best books of all time; you can only say they represent something about readers’ choices at a particular moment.

And yet like many others, I find these lists compulsive reading. I want to see if my favourites are on it, or if a book I hate is high on the list. Then I moan and groan and avidly wait for the next list to appear.

I find these book ranking lists compulsive reading. Getty Images/iStockphoto

The latest poll is from an ABC Radio National drive to find the 100 best Australian books of all time. This is a welcome antidote to international lists, which heavily favour American and British titles and rarely mention Australian books. You can nominate a shortlist of up to 10 books by October 1 and the final list will be announced live on a countdown on October 17 and 18.

I wonder what book will be number one? Possibly a Winton or a Garner or a Dalton or a Zusak – a book by a contemporary writer because these are the books most people read. Patrick White, long regarded as Australia’s best writer, is out of fashion. And whether we like it or not, fashion rules these lists.

Marnus Labuschagne is a man under siege, but insists he is not a spent force on the international stage as he fights to save his career in the Baggy Green. As he prepares to captain Queensland in their first one-day clash of the season against Victoria on Saturday, the Test No.3 also felt he still had a role to play in Australia’s limited overs side ahead of next year’s World Cup, despite being omitted from the squads to face Zimbabwe and South Africa. Labuschagne burst onto the scene in the Test arena and was at one stage ranked as the world’s best batsman. But his form woes over the past three years have been well documented – scoring just one century since the start of the 2023 Ashes, and averaging 26.27 since the start of that series. Marnus Labuschagne insists his game is “in good order”. Getty Images Those woes continued in August’s two-Test series against Bangladesh, with scores of one and 31 in Darwin followed by a limp dismissal for four in Mackay in which he strayed across his off stump and watched the ball cannon off his thigh guard and into his pegs.
