It has triggered widespread criticism and left his future in the side on shaky ground, with the likes of Australian great Ricky Ponting questioning his selection for the forthcoming three-Test series against the Proteas next month. Related Article Test cricket Sugar City to cricket centrepiece? How Mackay secured a historic Test, and its bold vision of what’s to come Labuschagne, however, stressed the chatter had not fazed him, as he vowed to right those wrongs in South Africa. “Criticism is part of the job if you want to be an international player. You can’t be sitting here going ‘I’m upset because people are criticising me.’ No one is criticising my character or my personality or who I am and what I stand for,” Labuschagne said on Friday, speaking from Allan Border Field as Queensland Cricket celebrated its 150th year. “They’re criticising my performance, and I’m the one who’s allowed that; because of the lack of performance, I’ve opened myself up to criticism. There’s clearly a reason why I’m still there, and I think the people who are in charge know that and know what I’ve done in the past for Australia.

“How I’ve performed the past two years is clearly not my standard and where I want to be, and I’m doing everything possible to make sure I get back there during this series in South Africa.” Labuschagne began the last domestic summer tipped to end his run of poor outputs on the biggest stage after striking two Sheffield Shield tons and four one-day centuries for the Bulls before the Ashes. But his inability to transfer that into the national colours cost him his 50-over spot. Marnus Labuschagne pictured for Australian in one-day cricket. AP From 23 ODI matches since the start of 2024, he has averaged just 21.88, having impressed as a middle order staple in 2023 (826 runs at 45.89). But the 32-year-old has sought a “silver lining” in his omission, adamant his chance to impress for Queensland and the opportunity to work closely with new Bulls coach James Hopes had given him ideal preparation time for South Africa. “Obviously, it’s always disappointing when you don’t get selected for Australia, but I’m also pretty experienced now, and I know my performances haven’t been where I needed them in international one-day cricket,” Labuschagne said.

“Last year I showed I’m playing very good domestic one-day cricket, and I’m not coming out here needing to prove to anyone I’m a good enough player. The 30-year-old earned a recall to the Test squad as an opener in place of Jake Weatherald, while he struck his maiden ODI hundred against Zimbabwe this week as a middle order anchor.

title: Decked out: How card games shuffled the everyday language of sports
text:
As a card-carrying member of the word nerd club, I can report that English has long been hooked on card games. Whether we hold the upper hand, pass the buck or offer a bargaining chip, our deck is stacked with table talk. Stacked in spades, with recent years only upping the ante.

Blame Trump, I guess. But that’s too simple a game, though trump (the verb) is Exhibit A, a corruption of triumph. Or triomphe in fact, a la the Parisian arch. A popular trick-taking game, triomphe is the forebear of euchre. The pastime fostered the idea of a trump card being your winning edge, the deal-clincher. Grand as that sounds, I love how NZ slang during WWI called anyone in authority, typically a cocky middle manager, as trump of the dump.

The English language has long been hooked on card games. iStock

Staying with US politics, Franklin D. Roosevelt’s New Deal offered a clean slate of social and economic reforms where tax revenue was above board – a further card-game borrowing. Despite that, any new deal will leave some citizens in the lurch, a phrase from cribbage. Lurch refers to an emphatic win where you “street” your opponent by more than twice their score. (Bear in mind that street is the column of peg-holes on a cribbage board, and nothing to do with Pennsylvania Avenue.) As for lurch, dictionary sleuth Michael Quinion suspects “lurz werden” to be the source, the German phrase meaning to become short.

At the stadium, table games and sport also meld, another verb drawn from the pack, canasta this time. In tennis, the US Open wraps the calendar of grand slams – a term via the bridge club. Just as we’re entering showdown season in football. And yes, showdown is another casino legacy. Poker on this occasion, when all the bluff and bluster is done, the stakes are high, demanding all players to lay down their hands, the showdown a sort of facing up.
